entries.087d06c4bfc45fee99952fdb5cc96ac8a96be3c2: <div sID="gen29705" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Acts.16" sID="Acts.16"/> <div eID="gen29705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29707" type="x-p"/> It is some rebuke to Barnabas that after he left Paul we hear no more of him, of what he did or suffered for Christ. But Paul, as he was recommended by the brethren to the grace of God, so his services for Christ after this are largely recorded; we are to attend him in this chapter from place to place, wherever he came doing good, either watering or planting, beginning new work or improving what was done. Here is, I. The beginning of his acquaintance with Timothy, and taking him to be his assistant, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1-Acts.16.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The visit he made to the churches for their establishment, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.4-Acts.16.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. His call to Macedonia (after a restraint he had been under from going to some other places), and his coming to Philippi, the chief city of Macedonia, with his entertainment there, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.6-Acts.16.13">ver. 6-13</reference>. IV. The conversion of Lydia there, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.14-Acts.16.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. V. The casing of an evil spirit out of a damsel, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.16-Acts.16.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. VI. The accusing and abusing of Paul and Silas for it, their imprisonment, and the indignities done them, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.19-Acts.16.24">ver. 19-24</reference>. VII. The miraculous conversion of the jailer to the faith of Christ, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.25-Acts.16.34">ver. 25-34</reference>. VIII. The honourable discharge of Paul and Silas by the magistrates, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.35-Acts.16.40">ver. 35-40</reference>.
entries.eca9b379db0574deb6ab165790e244bf549a2f32: <div eID="gen29707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29706" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Adoption of Timothy.</title> <div sID="gen29708" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then came he to Derbe and Lystra: and, behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus, the son of a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed; but his father <hi type="italic">was</hi> a Greek: <hi type="super">2</hi> Which was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium. <hi type="super">3</hi> Him would Paul have to go forth with him; and took and circumcised him because of the Jews which were in those quarters: for they knew all that his father was a Greek. <hi type="super">4</hi> And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem. <hi type="super">5</hi> And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily. <div eID="gen29708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29709" type="x-p"/> Paul was a spiritual father, and as such a one we have him here adopting Timothy, and taking care of the education of many others who had been begotten to Christ by his ministry: and in all he appears to have been a wise and tender father. Here is, <div eID="gen29709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29710" type="x-p"/> I. His taking Timothy into his acquaintance and under his tuition. One thing designed in the book of the Acts is to help us to understand Paul's epistles, two of which are directed to Timothy; it was therefore necessary that in the history of Paul we should have some account concerning him. And we are here accordingly told, 1. That he was a disciple, one that belonged to Christ, and was baptized, probably in his infancy, when his mother became a believer, as Lydia's household was baptized upon her believing, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.15">v. 15</reference>. Him, that was a disciple of Christ, Paul took to be his disciple, that he might further train him up in the knowledge and faith of Christ; he took him to be brought up for Christ. 2. That his mother was a Jewess originally, <hi type="italic">but believed in Christ;</hi> her name was <hi type="italic">Eunice,</hi> his grandmother's name was <hi type="italic">Lois.</hi> Paul speaks of them both with great respect, as women of eminent virtue and piety, and commends them especially for their unfeigned faith (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2 Tim. i. 5</reference>), their sincerely embracing and adhering to the doctrine of Christ. 3. That his father was a Greek, a Gentile. The marriage of a Jewish woman to a Gentile husband (though some would make a difference) was prohibited as much as the marriage of a Jewish man to a Gentile wife, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.3">Deut. vii. 3</reference>. Thou shalt no more <hi type="italic">give thy daughter to his son than take his daughter to thy son;</hi> yet this seems to have been limited to the nations that lived among them in Canaan, whom they were most in danger of infection from. Now because his father was a Greek he was not circumcised: for the entail of the covenant and the seal of it, as of other entails in that nation, went by the father, not by the mother; so that his father being no Jew he was not obliged to circumcision, nor entitled to it, unless when he grew up he did himself desire it. But, observe, though his mother could not prevail to have him circumcised in his infancy, because his father was of another mind and way, yet she educated him in the fear of God, that though he wanted the sign of the covenant he might not want the thing signified. 4. That he had gained a very good character among the Christians: he was <hi type="italic">well reported of by the brethren</hi> that were at Lystra and Iconium; he had not only an unblemished reputation, and was free from scandal, but he had a bright reputation, and great encomiums were given of him, as an extraordinary young man, and one from whom great things were expected. Not only those in the place where he was born, but those in the neighbouring cities, admired him, and spoke honourably of him. He had a name for good things with good people. 5. That Paul would have him <hi type="italic">to go forth with him,</hi> to accompany him, to give attendance on him, to receive instruction from him, and to join with him in the work of the gospel—to preach for him when there was occasion, and to be left behind in places where he had planted churches. Paul had a great love for him, not only because he was an ingenious young man, and one of great parts, but because he was a serious young man, and one of devout affections: for Paul was always <hi type="italic">mindful of his tears,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.4">2 Tim. i. 4</reference>. 6. That Paul took him and circumcised him, or ordered it to be done. This was strange. Had not Paul opposed those with all his might that were for imposing circumcision upon the Gentile converts? Had he not at this time the decrees of the council at Jerusalem with him, which witnessed against it? He had, and yet circumcised Timothy, not, as those teachers designed in imposing circumcision, to oblige him to keep the ceremonial law, but only to render his conversation and ministry passable, and, if it might be, acceptable among the Jews that abounded in those quarters. He knew Timothy was a man likely to do a great deal of good among them, being admirably qualified for the ministry, if they were not invincibly prejudiced against him; and therefore, that they might not shun him as one unclean, because uncircumcised, he took him and <hi type="italic">circumcised him.</hi> Thus <hi type="italic">to the Jews he became as a Jew, that he might gain the Jews,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all things to all men, that he might gain some.</hi> He was against those who made circumcision necessary to salvation, but used it himself when it was conducive to edification; nor was he rigid in opposing it, as they were in imposing it. Thus, though he went not in this instance according to the letter of the decree, he went according to the spirit of it, which was a spirit of tenderness towards the Jews, and willingness to bring them off gradually from their prejudices. Paul made no difficulty of taking Timothy to be his companion, though he was uncircumcised; but the Jews would not hear him if he were, and therefore Paul will humour them herein. It is probable that it was at this time that Paul laid his hands on Timothy, for the conferring of the gift of the Holy Ghost upon him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2 Tim. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen29710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29711" type="x-p"/> II. His confirming the churches which he had planted (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.4-Acts.16.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">He went through the cities</hi> where he had <hi type="italic">preached the word of the Lord,</hi> as he intended (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.36">ch. xv. 36</reference>), to enquire into their state. And we are told, <div eID="gen29711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29712" type="x-p"/> 1. That they delivered them copies of the decrees of the Jerusalem synod, to be a direction to them in the government of themselves, and that they might have wherewith to answer the judaizing teachers, and to justify themselves in adhering to the <hi type="italic">liberty with which Christ had made them free.</hi> All the churches were concerned in that decree, and therefore it was requisite they should all have it well attested. Though Paul had for a particular reason circumcised Timothy, yet he would not have that drawn into a precedent; and therefore he <hi type="italic">delivered the decrees</hi> to the churches, to be religiously observed; for they must abide by the rule, and not be drawn from it by a particular example. <div eID="gen29712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29713" type="x-p"/> 2. That this was of very good service to them. (1.) The churches were hereby <hi type="italic">established in the faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.5">v. 5</reference>. They were confirmed particularly in their opinion against the imposing of the ceremonial law upon the Gentiles; the great assurance and heat wherewith the judaizing teachers pressed the necessity of circumcision, and the plausible arguments they produced for it, had shocked them, so that they began to waver concerning it. But when they saw the testimony, not only of the apostles and elders, but of the Holy Ghost in them, against it, they were established, and did not longer waver about it. Note, Testimonies to truth, though they may not prevail to convince those that oppose it, may be of very good use to establish those that are in doubt concerning it, and to fix them. Nay, the design of this decree being to set aside the ceremonial law, and the carnal ordinances of that, they were by it established in the Christian faith in general, and were the more firmly assured that it was of God, because it set up a spiritual way of serving God, as more suited to the nature both of God and man; and, besides, that spirit of tenderness and condescension which appeared in these letters plainly showed that the apostles and elders were herein under the guidance of him who is love itself. (2.) They <hi type="italic">increased in number daily.</hi> The imposing of the yoke of the ceremonial law upon their converts was enough to frighten people from them. If they had been disposed to turn Jews, they could have done that long since, before the apostles came among them; but, if they cannot be interested in the Christian privileges without submitting to the Jews' yoke, they will be as they are. But, if they find there is no danger of their being so enslaved, they are ready to embrace Christianity, and join themselves to the church. And thus the church <hi type="italic">increased in numbers daily;</hi> not a day passed but some or other gave up their names to Christ. And it is a joy to those who heartily wish well to the honour of Christ, and the welfare of the church and the souls of men, to see such an increase.
entries.5c16b368faf7567a4204b308be47c59e84dee825: <div eID="gen29713" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul Invited into Macedonia; The Conversion of Lydia.</title> <div sID="gen29714" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia, <hi type="super">7</hi> After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not. 8 And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas. <hi type="super">9</hi> And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us. <hi type="super">10</hi> And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore loosing from Troas, we came with a straight course to Samothracia, and the next <hi type="italic">day</hi> to Neapolis; <hi type="super">12</hi> And from thence to Philippi, which is the chief city of that part of Macedonia, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a colony: and we were in that city abiding certain days. <hi type="super">13</hi> And on the sabbath we went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made; and we sat down, and spake unto the women which resorted <hi type="italic">thither.</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard <hi type="italic">us:</hi> whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul. <hi type="super">15</hi> And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought <hi type="italic">us,</hi> saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide <hi type="italic">there.</hi> And she constrained us. <div eID="gen29714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29715" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen29715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29716" type="x-p"/> I. Paul's travels up and down to do good. 1. He and Silas his colleague went throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, where, it should seem, the gospel was already planted, but whether by Paul's hand or no is not mentioned; it is likely it was, for in his epistle to the Galatians he speaks of his <hi type="italic">preaching the gospel to them at the first,</hi> and how very acceptable he was among them, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13-Gal.4.15">Gal. iv. 13-15</reference>. And it appears by that epistle that the judaizing teachers had then done a great deal of mischief to these churches of Galatia, had prejudiced them against Paul and drawn them from the gospel of Christ, for which he there severely reproves them. But probably that was a great while after this. 2. They were forbidden at this time to preach the gospel in Asia (the country properly so called), because it did not need, other hands being at work there; or because the people were not yet prepared to receive it, as they were afterwards (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.10">ch. xix. 10</reference>), when <hi type="italic">all those that dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord;</hi> or, as Dr. Lightfoot suggests, because at this time Christ would employ Paul in a piece of new work, which was to preach the gospel to a Roman colony at Philippi, for hitherto the Gentiles to whom he had preached were Greeks. The Romans were more particularly hated by the Jews than other Gentiles; their armies were the <hi type="italic">abomination of desolation;</hi> and therefore there is this among other things extraordinary in his call thither that he is forbidden to preach the gospel in Asia and other places, in order to his preaching it there, which is an intimation that the light of the gospel would in aftertimes be directed more westward than eastward. It was the Holy Ghost that forbade them, either by secret whispers in the minds of both of them, which, when they came to compare notes, they found to be the same, and to come from the same Spirit; or by some prophets who spoke to them from the Spirit. The removals of ministers, and the dispensing of the means of grace by them, are in a particular manner under a divine guidance and direction. We find an Old-Testament minister forbidden to preach at all (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.26">Ezek. iii. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be dumb.</hi> But these New-Testament ministers are only forbidden to preach in one place, while they are directed to another where there is more need. 3. They would have gone into Bithynia, but were not permitted: <hi type="italic">the Spirit suffered them not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.7">v. 7</reference>. They came to Mysia, and, as it should seem, preached the gospel there; for though it was a very mean contemptible country, even to a proverb (<hi type="italic">Mysorum ultimus,</hi> in Cicero, is <hi type="italic">a most despicable man</hi>), yet the apostles disdained not to visit it, owning themselves debtors both <hi type="italic">to the wise and to the unwise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.14">Rom. i. 14</reference>. In Bithynia was the city of Nice, where the first general council was held against the Arians; into these countries Peter sent his epistle (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1 Pet. i. 1</reference>); and there were flourishing churches here, for, though they had not the gospel sent them now, they had it in their turn, not long after. Observe, Though their judgment and inclination were to go into Bithynia, yet, having then extraordinary ways of knowing the mind of God, they were overruled by them, contrary to their own mind. We must now follow providence, and submit to the guidance of that pillar of cloud and fire; and, if this <hi type="italic">suffer us not</hi> to do what we assay to do, we ought to acquiesce, and believe it for the best. <hi type="italic">The Spirit of Jesus</hi> suffered them not; so many ancient copies read it. The servants of the Lord Jesus ought to be always under the check and conduct of the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord Jesus,</hi> by whom he governs men's minds. 4. They <hi type="italic">passed by Mysia,</hi> or passed <hi type="italic">through it</hi> (so some), sowing good seed, we may suppose, as they went along; and they came down to Troas, the city of Troy, so much talked of, or the country thereabouts, which took its denomination from it. Here a church was planted; for here we find one in being, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">ch. xx. 6, 7</reference>, and probably planted at this time, and in a little time. It should seem that at Troas Luke fell in with Paul, and joined himself to his company; for henceforward, for the most part, when he speaks of Paul's journeys, he puts himself into the number of his retinue, <hi type="italic">we</hi> went, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">v. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen29716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29717" type="x-p"/> II. Paul's particular call to Macedonia, that is, to Philippi, the chief city, inhabited mostly by Romans, as appears, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.21">v. 21</reference>. Here we have, <div eID="gen29717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29718" type="x-p"/> 1. The vision Paul had, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.9">v. 9</reference>. Paul had many visions, sometimes to encourage, sometimes, as here, to direct him in his work. An angel appeared to him, to intimate to him that it was the will of Christ he should go to Macedonia. Let him not be discouraged by the embargo laid upon him once and again, by which his designs were crossed; for, though he shall not go where he has a mind to go, he shall go where God has work for him to do. Now observe, (1.) The person Paul saw. There stood by him <hi type="italic">a man of Macedonia,</hi> who by his habit or dialect seemed so to Paul, or who told him he was so. The angel, some think, assumed the shape of such a man; or, as others think, impressed upon Paul's fancy, when between asleep and awake, the image of such a man: he dreamt he saw such a one. Christ would have Paul directed to Macedonia, not as the apostles were at other times, by a messenger from heaven, to send him thither, but by a messenger thence to call him thither, because in this way he would afterwards ordinarily direct the motions of his ministers, by inclining the hearts of those who needed them to invite them. Paul shall be called to Macedonia by a man of Macedonia, and by him speaking in the name of the rest. Some make this man to be the tutelar angel of Macedonia, supposing angels to have charge of particular places as well as persons, and that so much is intimated <reference osisRef="Dan.10.20">Dan. x. 20</reference>, where we read of the <hi type="italic">princes of Persia and Grecia,</hi> that seem to have been angels. But there is no certainty of this. There was presented either to Paul's eyes or to his mind a man of Macedonia. The angel must not preach the gospel himself to the Macedonians, but must bring Paul to them. Nor must he by the authority of an angel order him to go, but in the person of a Macedonian court him to come. A man of Macedonia, not a magistrate of the country, much less a priest (Paul was not accustomed to receive invitations from such) but an ordinary inhabitant of that country, a plain man, that carried in his countenance marks of probity and seriousness, that did not come to banter Paul nor trifle with him, but in good earnest and with all earnestness to importune his assistance. (2.) The invitation given him. This honest Macedonian <hi type="italic">prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us;</hi> that is, "Come and preach the gospel to us; let us have the benefit of thy labours." [1.] "<hi type="italic">Thou hast helped many;</hi> we have heard of those in this and the other country to whom thou hast been very useful; and why may we not put in for a share? O come and help us." The benefits others have received from the gospel should quicken our enquiries, our further enquiries, after it. [2.] "It is thy business, and it is thy delight, to help poor souls; thou art a physician for the sick, that art to be ready at the call of every patient; O come and help us." [3.] "We have need of thy help, as much as any people; we in Macedonia are as ignorant and as careless in religion as any people in the world are, are as idolatrous and as vicious as any, and as ingenious and industrious to ruin ourselves as any; and therefore, O come, come with all speed among us. <hi type="italic">If thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us.</hi>" [4.] "Those few among us that have any sense of divine things, and any concern for their own souls and the souls of others, have done what can be done, by the help of natural light; I have done my part for one. We have carried the matter as far as it will go, to persuade our neighbours to fear and worship God, but we can do little good among them. <hi type="italic">O come come, thou over, and help us.</hi> The gospel thou preachest has arguments and powers beyond those we have yet been furnished with." [5.] "Do not only help us with thy prayers here: this will not do; thou must come over and help us." Note, People have great need of help for their souls, and it is their duty to look out for it and invite those among them that can help them. <div eID="gen29718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29719" type="x-p"/> 2. The interpretation made of the vision (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">v. 10</reference>): They <hi type="italic">gathered assuredly from this that the Lord had called them to preach the gospel</hi> there; and they were ready to go wherever God directed. Note, We may sometimes infer a call of God from a call of man. If a man of Macedonia says, <hi type="italic">Come and help us,</hi> Paul thence gathers assuredly that God says, Go an help them. Ministers may go on with great cheerfulness and courage in their work when they perceive Christ calling them, not only to preach the gospel, but to preach it at this time, in this place, to this people. <div eID="gen29719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29720" type="x-p"/> III. Paul's voyage to Macedonia hereupon: He <hi type="italic">was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,</hi> but followed this divine direction much more cheerfully, and with more satisfaction, than he would have followed any contrivance or inclination of his own. 1. Thitherward he turned his thoughts. Now that he knows the mind of God in the matter he is determined, for this is all he wanted; now he thinks no more of Asia, nor Bithynia, but <hi type="italic">immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia.</hi> Paul only had the vision, but he communicated it to his companions, and they all, upon the credit of this, resolved for Macedonia. As Paul will follow Christ, so all his will follow him, or rather follow Christ with him. They are getting things in readiness for this expedition immediately, without delay. Note, God's calls must be complied with immediately. As our obedience must not be disputed, so it must not be deferred; do it to-day, lest thy heart be hardened. Observe, They could not immediately go into Macedonia; but they immediately endeavoured to go. If we cannot be so quick as we would be in our performances, yet we may be in our endeavours, and this shall be accepted. 2. Thitherward he steered his course. They <hi type="italic">set sail</hi> by the first shipping and with the first fair wind <hi type="italic">from Troas;</hi> for they may be sure they have done what they had to do there when God calls them to another place. They <hi type="italic">came with a straight course,</hi> a prosperous voyage, <hi type="italic">to Samothracia;</hi> the <hi type="italic">next day they came to Neapolis,</hi> a city on the confines of Thrace and Macedonia; and at last they landed at <hi type="italic">Philippi,</hi> a city so called from Philip king of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great; it is said (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.12">v. 12</reference>) to be, (1.) <hi type="italic">The chief city of that part of Macedonia;</hi> or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">the first city,</hi> the first they came to when they came from Troas. As an army that lands in a country of which they design to make themselves masters begin with the reduction of the first place they come to, so did Paul and his assistants: they began with the first city, because, if the gospel were received there, it would the more easily spread thence all the country over. (2.) It was a colony. The Romans not only had a garrison, but the inhabitants of the city were Romans, the magistrates at least, and the governing part. There were the greatest numbers and variety of people, and therefore the most likelihood of doing good. <div eID="gen29720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29721" type="x-p"/> IV. The cold entertainment which Paul and his companions met with at Philippi. One would have expected that having such a particular call from God thither they would have had a joyful welcome there, as Peter had with Cornelius when the angel sent him thither. Where was the man of Macedonia that begged Paul to come thither with all speed? Why did not he stir up his countrymen, some of them at least, to go and meet him? Why was not Paul introduced with solemnity, and the keys of the city put into his hand? Here is nothing like this; for, 1. It is a good while before any notice at all is taken of him: <hi type="italic">We were in that city abiding certain days,</hi> probably at a public house and at their own charge, for they had no friend to invite them so much as to a meal's meat, till Lydia welcomed them. They had made all the haste they could thither, but, now that they are there, they are almost tempted to think they might as well have staid where they were. But so it was ordered for their trial whether they could bear the pain of silence and lying by, when this was their lot. Those eminent and useful men are not fit to live in this world that know not how to be slighted and overlooked. Let not ministers think it strange if they be first strongly invited to a place, and then looked shyly upon when they come. 2. When they have an opportunity of preaching it is in an obscure place, and to a mean and small auditory, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.13">v. 13</reference>. There was no synagogue of the Jews there, for aught that appears, to be a door of entrance to them, and they never went to the idol-temples of the Gentiles, to preach to the auditories there; but here, upon enquiry, they found out a little meeting of good women, <hi type="italic">that were proselytes of the gate,</hi> who would be thankful to them if they would give them a sermon. The place of this meeting is out of the city; there it was connived at, but would not be suffered any where within the walls. It was a place <hi type="italic">where prayer was wont to be made;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proseuche</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">where an oratory or house of prayer was</hi> (so some), a chapel, or smaller synagogue. But I rather take it, as we read it, where prayer was appointed or accustomed to be. Those that worshipped the true God, and would not worship idols, met there to pray together, and, according to the description of the most ancient and universal devotion, <hi type="italic">to call upon the name of the Lord.</hi> Each of them prayed apart every day; this was always the practice of those that worshipped God: but, besides this, <hi type="italic">they came together on the sabbath day.</hi> Though they were but a few and discountenanced by the town, though their meeting was at some distance, though, for aught that appears, there were none but women, yet a solemn assembly the worshippers of God must have, if by any means it be possible, on the sabbath day. When we cannot do as we would we must do as we can; if we have not synagogues, we must be thankful for more private places, and resort to them, <hi type="italic">not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together,</hi> according as our opportunities are. This place is said to be <hi type="italic">by a river side,</hi> which perhaps was chosen, as befriending contemplation. Idolaters are said <hi type="italic">to take their lot among the smooth stones of the stream,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.6">Isa. lvii. 6</reference>. But these proselytes had in their eye, perhaps, the example of those prophets who had their visions, one by the <hi type="italic">river of Chebar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.1">Ezek. i. 1</reference>), another by <hi type="italic">the great river Hiddekel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.4">Dan. x. 4</reference>. Thither Paul and Silas and Luke went, and <hi type="italic">sat down,</hi> to instruct the congregation, that they might the better pray with them. They <hi type="italic">spoke unto the women who resorted thither,</hi> encouraged them in practising according to the light they had, and led them on further to the knowledge of Christ. <div eID="gen29721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29722" type="x-p"/> V. The conversion of <hi type="italic">Lydia,</hi> who probably was the first that was wrought upon there to believe in Christ, though not the last. In this story of <hi type="italic">the Acts,</hi> we have not only the conversion of places recorded, but of many particular persons; for such is the worth of souls that the reducing of one to God is a great matter. Nor have we only the conversions that were effected by miracle, as Paul's, but some that were brought about by the ordinary methods of grace, as Lydia's here. Observe, <div eID="gen29722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29723" type="x-p"/> 1. Who this convert was that there is such particular notice taken of. Four things are recorded of her:— <div eID="gen29723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29724" type="x-p"/> (1.) Her name, <hi type="italic">Lydia.</hi> It is an honour to her to have her name recorded here in the book of God, so that <hi type="italic">wherever the scriptures are read there shall this be told concerning her.</hi> Note, The names of the saints are precious with God, and should be so with us; we cannot have our names recorded in the Bible, but, if God open our hearts, we shall find them <hi type="italic">written in the book of life,</hi> and this is better (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">Phil. iv. 3</reference>) and more to <hi type="italic">be rejoiced in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Luke x. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen29724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29725" type="x-p"/> (2.) Her calling. She was <hi type="italic">a seller of purple,</hi> either of purple dye or of purple cloth or silk. Observe, [1.] She had a calling, an honest calling, which the historian takes notice of to her praise; she was none of those women that the apostle speaks of (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">1 Tim. v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">who learn to be idle, and not only idle, &c.</hi> [2.] It was a mean calling. She was <hi type="italic">a seller of purple,</hi> not a wearer of purple, few such are called. The notice here taken of this is an intimation to those who are employed in honest callings, if they be honest in the management of them, not to be ashamed of them. [3.] Though she had a calling to mind, yet she was a worshipper of God, and found time to improve advantages for her soul. The business of our particular callings may be made to consist very well with the business of religion, and therefore it will not excuse us from religious exercises alone, and in our families, or in solemn assemblies, to say, We have shops to look after, and a trade to mind; for have we not also a God to serve and a soul to look after? Religion does not call us from our business in the world, but directs us in it. Every thing in its time and place. <div eID="gen29725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29726" type="x-p"/> (3.) The place she was of—<hi type="italic">of the city of Thyatira,</hi> which was a great way from Philippi; there she was born and bred, but either married at Philippi, or brought by her trade to settle there. The providence of God, as it always appoints, so it often removes, <hi type="italic">the bounds of our habitation,</hi> and sometimes makes the change of our outward condition or place of our abode wonderfully subservient to the designs of his grace concerning our salvation. Providence brings Lydia to Philippi, to be under Paul's ministry, and there, where she met with it, she made a good use of it; so should we improve opportunities. <div eID="gen29726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29727" type="x-p"/> (4.) Her religion before the Lord opened her heart. [1.] She worshipped God according to the knowledge she had; she was one of the devout women. Sometimes the grace of God wrought upon those who, before their conversion, were very wicked and vile, publicans and harlots; <hi type="italic">such were some of you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>. But sometimes it fastened upon those who were of a good character, who had some good in them, as the eunuch, Cornelius, and Lydia. Note, It is not enough to be worshippers of God, but we must be believers in Jesus Christ, for there is no coming to God as a Father, but by him as Mediator. But those who worshipped God according to the light they had stood fair for the discoveries of Christ, and his grace to them; for <hi type="italic">to him that has shall be given:</hi> and to them Christ would be welcome; for those that know what it is to worship God see their need of Christ, and know what use to make of his mediation. [2.] She heard the apostles. Here, where prayer was made, when there was an opportunity, <hi type="italic">the word was preached;</hi> for hearing the word of God is a part of religious worship, and how can we expect God should hear our prayers if we will not hearken to his word? Those that worshipped God according to the light they had looked out for further light; we must improve <hi type="italic">the day of small things,</hi> but must not rest in it. <div eID="gen29727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29728" type="x-p"/> 2. What the work was that was wrought upon her: <hi type="italic">Whose heart the Lord opened.</hi> Observe here, (1.) The author of this work: it was <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi>—the Lord Christ, to whom this judgment is committed,—the Spirit of the Lord, who is the sanctifier. Note, Conversion-work is God's work; it is he <hi type="italic">that works in us both to will and to do;</hi> not as if we had nothing to do, but of ourselves, without God's grace, we can do nothing; nor as if God were in the least chargeable with the ruin of those that perish, but the salvation of those that are saved must be wholly ascribed to him. (2.) The seat of this work; it is in the heart that the change is made, it is to the heart that this blessed turn is given; it was the heart of Lydia that was wrought upon. Conversion-work is heart-work; it is a <hi type="italic">renewing of the heart, the inward man, the spirit of the mind.</hi> (3.) The nature of the work; she had not only her heart touched, but her heart opened. An unconverted soul is shut up, and fortified against Christ, <hi type="italic">straitly shut up,</hi> as Jericho against Joshua, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.1">Josh. vi. 1</reference>. Christ, in dealing with the soul, knocks at the door that is shut against him (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>); and, when a sinner is effectually persuaded to embrace Christ, <hi type="italic">then the heart is opened for the King of glory to come in</hi>—the understanding is open to receive the divine light, the will opened to receive the divine law, and the affections opened to receive the divine love. When the heart is thus opened to Christ, the ear is opened to his word, the lips opened in prayer, the hand opened in charity, and the steps enlarged in all manner of gospel obedience. <div eID="gen29728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29729" type="x-p"/> 3. What were the effects of this work on the heart. (1.) She took great notice of the word of God. Her heart was so <hi type="italic">opened that she attended to the things that were spoken by Paul;</hi> she not only gave attendance on Paul's preaching, but gave attention to it; <hi type="italic">she applied to herself</hi> (so some read it) <hi type="italic">the things that were spoken by Paul;</hi> and then only the word does us good, and makes an abiding impression upon us, when we apply it to ourselves. Now this was an evidence of the opening of her heart, and was the fruit of it; wherever the heart is opened by the grace of God, it will appear by a diligent attendance on, and attention to, the word of God, both for Christ's sake, whose word it is, and for our own sakes, who are so nearly interested in it. (2.) She gave up her name to Jesus Christ, and took upon her the profession of his holy religion; <hi type="italic">She was baptized,</hi> and by this solemn rite was admitted a member of the church of Christ; and with her <hi type="italic">her household</hi> also was baptized, those of them that were infants in her right, for if <hi type="italic">the root be holy so are the branches,</hi> and those that were grown up by her influence and authority. She and her household were baptized by the same rule that Abraham and his household were circumcised, because the seal of the covenant belongs to the covenanters and their seed. (3.) She was very kind to the ministers, and very desirous to be further instructed by them in <hi type="italic">the things pertaining to the kingdom of God: She besought us saying "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord,</hi> if you take me to be a sincere Christian, manifest your confidence in me by this, <hi type="italic">come into my house, and abide there.</hi>" Thus she desired an opportunity, [1.] To testify her gratitude to those who had been the instruments of divine grace in this blessed change that was wrought upon her. When her heart was open to Christ, her house was open to his ministers for his sake, and they were welcome to the best entertainment she had, which she did not think too good for those of whose spiritual things she had reaped so plentifully. Nay, they are not only welcome to her house, but she is extremely pressing and importunate with them: <hi type="italic">She constrained us;</hi> which intimates that Paul was very backward and unwilling to go, because he was afraid of being burdensome to the families of the young converts, and would study <hi type="italic">to make the gospel of Christ without charge</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.18">1 Cor. ix. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.34">Acts xx. 34</reference>), that those who were without might have no occasion given them to reproach the preachers of the gospel as designing, self-seeking men, and that those who were within might have no occasion to complain of the expenses of their religion: but Lydia will have no nay; she will not believe that they take her to be a sincere Christian unless they will oblige her herein; like Abraham inviting the angels (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.3">Gen. xviii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">If now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away from thy servant.</hi> [2.] She desired an opportunity of receiving further instruction. If she might but have them for awhile in her family, she might hear them daily (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.34">Prov. viii. 34</reference>), and not merely on sabbath days at the meeting. In her own house she might not only hear them, but ask them questions; and she might have them to pray with her daily, and to bless her household. Those that know something of Christ cannot but desire to know more, and seek opportunities of increasing their acquaintance with his gospel.
entries.aff10eba90c6e80df218adcc291f94ee9df5531e: <div eID="gen29729" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Expulsion of an Evil Spirit; Persecution of Philippi.</title> <div sID="gen29730" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass, as we went to prayer, a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met us, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying: <hi type="super">17</hi> The same followed Paul and us, and cried, saying, These men are the servants of the most high God, which show unto us the way of salvation. 18 And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone, they caught Paul and Silas, and drew <hi type="italic">them</hi> into the marketplace unto the rulers, <hi type="super">20</hi> And brought them to the magistrates, saying, These men, being Jews, do exceedingly trouble our city, <hi type="super">21</hi> And teach customs, which are not lawful for us to receive, neither to observe, being <reference osisRef="Rom.22">Romans. 22</reference> And the multitude rose up together against them: and the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">23</hi> And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely: <hi type="super">24</hi> Who, having received such a charge, thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks. <div eID="gen29730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29731" type="x-p"/> Paul and his companions, though they were for some time buried in obscurity at Philippi, yet now begin to be taken notice of. <div eID="gen29731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29732" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">A damsel that had a spirit of divination</hi> caused them to be taken notice of, by proclaiming them to be the servants of God. Observe, <div eID="gen29732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29733" type="x-p"/> 1. The account that is given of this damsel: She was <hi type="italic">pythonissa, possessed with</hi> such <hi type="italic">a spirit of divination</hi> as that damsel was by whom the oracles of Apollo at Delphos were delivered; she was actuated by an evil spirit, that dictated ambiguous answers to those who consulted her, which served to gratify their vain desire of knowing things to come, but often deceived them. In those times of ignorance, infidelity, and idolatry, the devil, by the divine permission, thus led men captive at his will; and he could not have gained such adoration from them as he had, if he had not pretended to give oracles to them, for by both his usurpation is maintained as the god of this world. This damsel <hi type="italic">brought her masters much gain by soothsaying;</hi> many came to consult this witch for the discovery of robberies, the finding of things lost, and especially to be told their fortune, and none came but with the rewards of divination in their hands, according to the quality of the person and the importance of the case. Probably there were many that were thus kept for fortune-tellers, but, it should seem, this was more in repute than any of them; for, while others brought some gain, this <hi type="italic">brought much gain to her masters,</hi> being consulted more than any other. <div eID="gen29733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29734" type="x-p"/> 2. The testimony which this damsel gave to Paul and his companions: She <hi type="italic">met them</hi> in the street, as they were going to prayer, to the house of prayer, or rather to the work of prayer there, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.16">v. 16</reference>. They went thither publicly, every body knew whither they were going, and what they were going to do. If what she did was likely to be any distraction to them, or a hindrance in their work, it is observable how subtle Satan is, that great tempter, in taking the opportunity to give us diversion when we are going about any religious exercises, to ruffle us and to put us out of temper when we need to be most composed. When she met with them she followed them, crying, "<hi type="italic">These men,</hi> how contemptible soever they look and are looked upon, are great men, for they <hi type="italic">are the servants of the most high God,</hi> and men that should be very welcome to us, for <hi type="italic">they show unto us the way of salvation,</hi> both the salvation that will be our happiness, and the way to it that will be our holiness." <div eID="gen29734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29735" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) This witness is true; it is a comprehensive encomium on the faithful preachers of the gospel, and makes their feet beautiful, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Rom. x. 15</reference>. Though they are <hi type="italic">men subject to like passions as we are,</hi> and <hi type="italic">earthen vessels,</hi> yet, [1.] "They are <hi type="italic">the servants of the most high God;</hi> they attend on him, are employed by him, and are devoted to his honour, as servants; they come to us on his errands, the message they bring is from him, and they serve the purposes and interest of his kingdom. The gods we Gentiles worship are inferior beings, therefore not gods, but these men belong to the supreme <hi type="italic">Numen, to the most high God,</hi> who is over all men, over all gods, who made us all, and to whom we are all accountable. They are his servants, and therefore it is our duty to respect them, and harken to them for their Master's sake, and it is at our peril if we affront them." [2.] "They <hi type="italic">show unto us the way of salvation.</hi>" Even the heathen had some notion of the miserable deplorable state of mankind, and their need of salvation, and it was what they made some enquiries after. "Now," saith she, "these men are the men that show us what we have in vain sought for in our superstitious profitless application to our priests and oracles." Note, God has, in the gospel of his Son, plainly shown us the way of salvation, has told us what we must do that we may be delivered from the misery to which by sin we have exposed ourselves. <div eID="gen29735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29736" type="x-p"/> But, (2.) How came this testimony from the mouth of one that had a spirit of divination? Is Satan divided against himself? Will he cry up those whose business it is to pull him down? We may take it either, [1.] As extorted from this spirit of divination for the honour of the gospel by the power of God; as the devil was forced to say of Christ (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">Mark i. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God.</hi> The truth is sometimes magnified by the confession of its adversaries, in which they are witnesses against themselves. Christ would have this testimony of the damsel to rise up in judgment against those at Philippi who slighted and persecuted the apostles; though the gospel needed no such testimony, yet it shall serve to add to their commendation that the damsel whom they looked upon as an oracle in other things proclaimed the apostles God's servants. Or, [2.] As designed by the evil spirit, that subtle serpent, to the dishonour of the gospel; some think she designed hereby to gain credit to herself and her prophecies, and so to increase her master's profit by pretending to be in the interest of the apostles, who, she thought, had a growing reputation, or to curry favour with Paul, that he might not separate her and her familiar. Others think that Satan, who can transform himself into an angel of light, and can say anything to serve a turn, designed hereby to disgrace the apostles; as if these divines were of the same fraternity with their diviners, because they were witnessed to by them, and then the people might as well adhere to those they had been used to. Those that were most likely to receive the apostles' doctrine were such as were prejudiced against these spirits of divination, and therefore would, by this testimony, be prejudiced against the gospel; and, as for those who regarded these diviners, the devil thought himself sure of them. <div eID="gen29736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29737" type="x-p"/> II. Christ caused them to be taken notice of, by giving them power to cast the devil out of this damsel. She continued <hi type="italic">many days</hi> clamouring thus (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.18">v. 18</reference>); and, it should seem, Paul took no notice of her, not knowing but it might be ordered of God for the service of his cause, that she should thus witness concerning his ministers; but finding perhaps that it did them a prejudice, rather than any service, he soon silenced her, by casting the devil out of her. 1. He was <hi type="italic">grieved.</hi> It troubled him to see the damsel made an instrument of Satan to deceive people, and to see the people imposed upon by her divinations. It was a disturbance to him to hear a sacred truth so profaned, and good words come out of such a wicked mouth with such and evil design. Perhaps they were spoken in an ironical bantering way, as ridiculing the apostles' pretensions, and mocking them, as when Christ's persecutors complimented him with <hi type="italic">Hail, king of the Jews;</hi> and then justly might Paul be grieved, as any good man's heart would be, to hear any good truth of God bawled out in the streets in a canting jeering way. 2. He <hi type="italic">commanded the evil spirit to come out of her. He turned</hi> with a holy indignation, angry both at the flatteries and at the reproaches of <hi type="italic">the unclean spirit, and said, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her;</hi> and by this he will show <hi type="italic">that these men are the servants of the living God,</hi> and are able to prove themselves so, without her testimony: her silence shall demonstrate it more than her speaking could do. Thus Paul shows <hi type="italic">the way of salvation</hi> indeed, that it is by breaking <hi type="italic">the power of Satan, and chaining him up, that he may not deceive the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">Rev. xx. 3</reference>), and that this salvation is to be obtained <hi type="italic">in the name of Jesus Christ</hi> only, as in his name the devil was now cast out and by no other. It was a great blessing to the country when Christ by a word cast the devil out of those in whom he frightened people and molested them <hi type="italic">so that no man might pass by that way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.28">Matt. viii. 28</reference>); but it was a much greater kindness to the country when Paul now, in Christ's name, cast the devil out of one who deceived people and imposed upon their credulity. Power went along with the word of Christ, before which Satan could not stand, but was forced to quit his hold, and in this case it was a strong hold: <hi type="italic">He came out the same hour.</hi> <div eID="gen29737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29738" type="x-p"/> III. The masters of the damsel that was dispossessed caused them to be taken notice of, by bringing them before the magistrates for doing it, and laying it to their charge as their crime. The preachers of the gospel would never have had an opportunity of speaking to the magistrates if they had not been brought before them as evil doers. Observe here, <div eID="gen29738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29739" type="x-p"/> 1. That which provoked them was, that, the damsel being restored to herself, <hi type="italic">her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.19">v. 19</reference>. See here what evil <hi type="italic">the love of money is the root of!</hi> If the preaching of the gospel ruin the craft of the silversmiths (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.24">ch. xix. 24</reference>), much more the craft of the soothsayers; and therefore here is a great outcry raised, when Satan's power to deceive is broken: the priests hated the gospel because it turned men from the blind service of dumb idols, and so the hope of their gains was gone. The power of Christ, which appeared in dispossessing the woman, and the great kindness done to her in delivering her out of Satan's hand, made no impression upon them when they apprehended that they should hereby lose money. <div eID="gen29739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29740" type="x-p"/> 2. The course they took with them was to incense the higher powers against them, as men fit to be punished: <hi type="italic">They caught them</hi> as they went along, and, with the utmost fury and violence, <hi type="italic">dragged them into the marketplace,</hi> where public justice was administered. (1.) They brought them <hi type="italic">to the rulers,</hi> their justices of peace, to do by them as men taken into the hands of the law, the <hi type="italic">duumviri.</hi> (2.) From them they hurried them <hi type="italic">to the magistrates,</hi> the prætors or governors of the city, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tois strategois</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the officers of the army,</hi> so the word signifies; but it is taken in general for the judges or chief rulers: to them they brought their complaint. <div eID="gen29740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29741" type="x-p"/> 3. The charge they exhibited against them was that they were the troublers of the land, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.20">v. 20</reference>. They take it for granted that these men are Jews, a nation at this time as much an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Romans</hi> as they had long ago been to the Egyptians. Piteous was the case of the apostles, when it was turned to their reproach that they were Jews, and yet the Jews were their most violent persecutors! (1.) The general charge against them is <hi type="italic">that they troubled the city,</hi> sowed discord, and disturbed the public peace, and occasioned riots and tumults, than which nothing could be more false and unjust, as was Ahab's character of Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">1 Kings xviii. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Art thou he that troubleth Israel?</hi> If they troubled the city, it was but like the angel's troubling the water of Bethesda's pool, in order to healing-shaking, in order to a happy settlement. Thus those that rouse the sluggards are exclaimed against for troubling them. (2.) The proof of this charge is their teaching customs not proper to be admitted by a Roman colony, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.21">v. 21</reference>. The Romans were always very jealous of innovations in religion. Right or wrong, they would adhere to that, how vain soever, which they had received by tradition from their fathers. No foreign nor upstart deity must be allowed, without the approbation of the senate; the gods of their country must be their gods, true or false. This was one of the laws of the twelve tables. <hi type="italic">Hath a nation changed their gods?</hi> It incensed them against the apostles that they taught a religion destructive of polytheism and idolatry, and preached to them to turn from those vanities. This the Romans could not bear: "If this grow upon us, in a little while we shall lose our religion." <div eID="gen29741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29742" type="x-p"/> IV. The magistrates, by their proceedings against them, caused them to be taken notice of. <div eID="gen29742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29743" type="x-p"/> 1. By countenancing the persecution they raised the mob upon them (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">The multitude rose up together against them,</hi> and were ready to pull them to pieces. It has been the artifice of Satan to make God's ministers and people odious to the commonalty, by representing them as dangerous men, who aimed at the destruction of the constitution and the changing of the customs, when really there has been no ground for such an imputation. <div eID="gen29743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29744" type="x-p"/> 2. By going on to an execution they further represented them as the vilest malefactors: <hi type="italic">They rent off their clothes,</hi> with rage and fury, not having patience till they were taken off, in order to their being scourged. This the apostle refers to when he speaks of <hi type="italic">their being treated at Philippi,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1 Thess. ii. 2</reference>. The magistrates commanded that they should be whipped as vagabonds, by the lictors or beadles who attended the prætors, and carried rods with them for that purpose; this was one of those three times that Paul was beaten with rods, according to the Roman usage, which was not under the compassionate limitation of the number of stripes not to exceed forty, which was provided by the Jewish law. It is here said that <hi type="italic">they laid many stripes upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.23">v. 23</reference>), without counting how many, because they seemed vile unto them, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.3">Deut. xxv. 3</reference>. Now, one would think, this might have satiated their cruelty; if they must be whipped, surely they must be discharged. No, they are imprisoned, and it is probable the present purpose was to try them for their lives, and put them to death; else why should there be such care taken to prevent their escape? (1.) The judges made their commitment very strict: They <hi type="italic">charged the jailer to keep them safely,</hi> and have a very watchful eye upon them, as if they were dangerous men, that either would venture to break prison themselves or were in confederacy with those that would attempt to rescue them. Thus they endeavoured to render them odious, that they might justify themselves in the base usage they had given them. (2.) The jailer made their confinement very severe (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Having received such a charge,</hi> though he might have kept them safely enough in the outer prison, yet <hi type="italic">he thrust them into the inner prison.</hi> He was sensible that the magistrates had a great indignation against these men, and were inclined to be severe with them, and therefore he thought to ingratiate himself with them, by exerting his power likewise against them to the uttermost. When magistrates are cruel, it is no wonder that the officers under them are so too. <hi type="italic">He put them into the inner prison,</hi> the dungeon, into which none were usually put but condemned malefactors, dark at noon-day, damp and cold, dirty, it is likely, and every way offensive, like that into which Jeremiah was let down (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jer. xxxviii. 6</reference>); and, as if this were not enough, <hi type="italic">he made their feet fast in the stocks.</hi> Perhaps, having heard a report of the escape of <hi type="italic">the preachers of the gospel out of prison, when the doors were fast barred</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.19">ch. v. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.19">xii. 9</reference>), he thought he would be wiser than other jailers had been, and therefore would effectually secure them by fastening them in the stocks; and they were not the first of God's messengers that had their feet in the stocks; Jeremiah was so treated, and publicly too, in <hi type="italic">the high-gate of Benjamin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.2">Jer. xx. 2</reference>); Joseph had his <hi type="italic">feet hurt with fetters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.18">Ps. cv. 18</reference>. Oh what hard usage have God's servants met with, as in the former days, so in the latter times! Witness the Book of Martyrs, martyrs in queen Mary's time.
entries.ab17534956e6c8ab83f66e5ade372204f2dba5e4: <div eID="gen29744" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul and Silas in Prison; Conversion of the Philippian Jailer.</title> <div sID="gen29745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them. <hi type="super">26</hi> And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled. <hi type="super">28</hi> But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas, <hi type="super">30</hi> And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? <hi type="super">31</hi> And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. <hi type="super">32</hi> And they spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed <hi type="italic">their</hi> stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway. <hi type="super">34</hi> And when he had brought them into his house, he set meat before them, and rejoiced, believing in God with all his house. <div eID="gen29745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29746" type="x-p"/> We have here the designs of the persecutors of Paul and Silas baffled and broken. <div eID="gen29746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29747" type="x-p"/> I. The persecutors designed to dishearten and discourage the preachers of the gospel, and to make them sick of the cause and weary of their work; but here we find them both hearty and heartened. <div eID="gen29747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29748" type="x-p"/> 1. They were themselves hearty, wonderfully hearty; never were poor prisoners so truly cheerful, nor so far from laying their hard usage to heart. Let us consider what their case was. The prætors among the Romans had rods carried before them, and axes bound upon them, the <hi type="italic">fasces and secures.</hi> Now they had felt the smart of the rods, <hi type="italic">the ploughers had ploughed upon their backs, and made long furrows.</hi> The many stripes they had laid upon them were very sore, and one might have expected to hear them complaining of them, of the rawness and soreness of their backs and shoulders. Yet this was not all; they had reason to fear the axes next. Their master was first scourged and then crucified; and they might expect the same. In the mean time they were in the inner prison, their feet in the stocks, which, some think, not only held them, but hurt them; and yet, <hi type="italic">at midnight,</hi> when they should have been trying, if possible, to get a little rest, they <hi type="italic">prayed and sang praises to God.</hi> (1.) They prayed together, prayed to God to support them and comfort them in their afflictions, to visit them, as he did Joseph in the prison, and to be with them,—prayed that their consolations in Christ might abound, as their afflictions for him did,—prayed that even their bonds and stripes might turn to the furtherance of the gospel,—prayed for their persecutors, that God would forgive them and turn their hearts. This was not at an hour of prayer, but at midnight; it was not in a house of prayer, but in a dungeon; yet it was seasonable to pray, and the prayer was acceptable. As in the dark, so out of the depths, we may cry unto God. No place, no time, amiss for prayer, if the heart be lifted up to God. Those that are companions in suffering should join in prayer. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? Let him pray.</hi> No trouble, how grievous soever, should indispose us for prayer. (2.) <hi type="italic">They sang praises to God.</hi> They praised God; for we must <hi type="italic">in every thing give thanks.</hi> We never want matter for praise, if we do not want a heart. And what should put the heart of a child of God out of tune for this duty if a dungeon and a pair of stocks will not do it? They praised God that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name, and that they were so wonderfully supported and borne up under their sufferings, and felt divine consolations so sweet, so strong, in their souls. Nay, <hi type="italic">they not only praised God, but they sang praises to him,</hi> in some psalm, or hymn, or spiritual song, either one of David's, or some modern composition, or one of their own, as <hi type="italic">the Spirit gave them utterance.</hi> As our rule is that the afflicted should pray, and therefore, being in affliction, they prayed; so our rule is that the merry should sing psalms (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">James v. 13</reference>), and therefore, being merry in their affliction, <hi type="italic">merry after a godly sort, they sang psalms.</hi> This proves that the singing of psalms is a gospel ordinance, and ought to be used by all good Christians; and that it is instituted, not only for the expressing of their joys in a day of triumph, but for the balancing and relieving of their sorrows in a day of trouble. It was at midnight that they sang psalms, according to the example of the sweet psalmist of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.62">Ps. cxix. 62</reference>): <hi type="italic">At midnight will I rise to give thanks unto thee.</hi> (3.) Notice is here taken of the circumstance that <hi type="italic">the prisoners heard them.</hi> If the prisoners did not hear them pray, yet <hi type="italic">they heard them sing praises.</hi> [1.] It intimates how hearty they were in singing praises to God; they sang so loud that, though they were in the dungeon, they were heard all the prison over; nay, so loud that they woke the prisoners: for we may suppose, being at midnight, they were all asleep. We should sing psalms with all our heart. The saints are called upon to sing aloud upon their beds, <reference osisRef="Ps.149.5">Ps. cxlix. 5</reference>. But gospel grace carries the matter further, and gives us an example of those that sang aloud in the prison, in the stocks. [2.] Though they knew the prisoners would hear them, yet they sang aloud, as those that were not ashamed of their Master, nor of his service. Shall those that would sing psalms in their families plead, in excuse for their omission of the duty, that they are afraid their neighbours should hear them, when those that sing profane songs roar them our, and care not who hears them? [3.] The prisoners were made to hear the prison-songs of Paul and Silas, that they might be prepared for the miraculous favour shown to them all for the sake of Paul and Silas, when <hi type="italic">the prison-doors were thrown open.</hi> By this extraordinary comfort with which they were filled it was published that he whom they preached was <hi type="italic">the consolation of Israel.</hi> Let the prisoners that mean to oppose him hear and tremble before him; let those that are faithful to him hear and triumph, and take of the comfort that is spoken to the prisoners of hope, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.12">Zech. ix. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen29748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29749" type="x-p"/> 2. God heartened them wonderfully by his signal appearances for them, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.26">v. 26</reference>. (1.) There was immediately a great earthquake; how far it extended we are not told, but it was such a violent shock in this place <hi type="italic">that the very foundations of the prison were shaken.</hi> While the prisoners were hearkening to the midnight devotions of Paul and Silas, and perhaps laughing at them and making a jest of them, this earthquake would strike a terror upon them, and convince them that those men were the favourites of Heaven, and such as God owned. We had <hi type="italic">the house of prayer shaken,</hi> in answer to prayer, and as a token of God's acceptance of it, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.31">ch. iv. 31</reference>. Here <hi type="italic">the prison shaken.</hi> The Lord was in these earthquakes, to show his resentment of the indignities done to his servants, to testify to those whose confidence is in the earth the weakness and instability of that which they confide, and to teach people <hi type="italic">that, though the earth be moved, yet they need not fear.</hi> (2.) The prison-doors were thrown open, and the prisoners' fetters were knocked off: <hi type="italic">Every man's bands were loosed.</hi> Perhaps the prisoners, when they heard Paul and Silas pray and sing psalms, admired them, and spoke honourably of them, and said what the damsel had said of them, Surely, <hi type="italic">these men are the servants of the living God.</hi> To recompense them for, and confirm them in, their good opinion of them, they share in the miracle, and have <hi type="italic">their bands loosed;</hi> as afterwards God gave to Paul all <hi type="italic">those that were in the ship with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.24">ch. xxvii. 24</reference>), so now he gave him all those that were in the prison with him. God hereby signified to these prisoners, as Grotius observes, that the apostles, in preaching the gospel, were public blessings to mankind, as they <hi type="italic">proclaimed liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison-doors to those that were bound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Et per eos solvi animorum vincula—and as by them the bonds of souls were unloosed.</hi> <div eID="gen29749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29750" type="x-p"/> II. The persecutors designed to stop the progress of the gospel, that no more might embrace it; thus they hoped to ruin the meeting by the river side, that no more hearts should be opened there; but here we find converts made in the prison, that house turned into a meeting, the trophies of the gospel's victories erected there, and the jailer, their own servant, become a servant of Christ. It is probable that some of the prisoners, if not all, were converted; surely the miracle wrought on their bodies, in loosing their bands, was wrought on their souls too. See <reference osisRef="Job.36.8-Job.36.10">Job xxxvi. 8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.14-Ps.107.15">Ps. cvii. 14, 15</reference>. But it is only the conversion of the jailer that is recorded. <div eID="gen29750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29751" type="x-p"/> 1. He is afraid he shall lose his life, and Paul makes him easy as to this care, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.27-Acts.16.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. (1.) He <hi type="italic">awoke out of his sleep.</hi> It is probable that the shock of the earthquake woke him, and the opening of the prison-doors, and the prisoners' expressions of joy and amazement, when in the dark they found their bands loosed, and called to tell one another what they felt: this was enough to awaken the jailer, whose place required that he should not be hard to wake. This waking him out of his sleep signified the awakening of his conscience out of its spiritual slumber. The call of the gospel is, <hi type="italic">Awake, thou that sleepest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Eph. v. 14</reference>), like that of <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.6">Jonah, i. 6</reference>. (2.) He saw the prison-doors open, and supposed, as well he might, that the prisoners had fled; and then what would become of him? He knew the Roman law in that case, and it was executed not long ago upon the keepers out of whose hands Peter escaped, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.19">ch. xii. 19</reference>. It was according to that of the prophet, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.39">1 Kings xx. 39</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.42">42</reference>, <hi type="italic">Keep this man; if he be missing, thy life shall go for his life.</hi> The Roman lawyers after this, in their readings upon the law, <hi type="italic">De custodia reorum—The custody of criminals</hi> (which appoints that the keeper should undergo the same punishment that should have been inflicted on the prisoner if he let him escape), take care to except an escape by miracle. (3.) In his fright <hi type="italic">he drew his sword,</hi> and was going <hi type="italic">to kill himself,</hi> to prevent a more terrible death, and expected one, a pompous ignominious death, which he knew he was liable to for letting his prisoners escape and not looking better to them; and the extraordinarily strict charge which the magistrates gave him concerning Paul and Silas made him conclude they would be very severe upon him if they were gone. The philosophers generally allowed self-murder. Seneca prescribes it as the last remedy which those that are in distress may have recourse to. The Stoics, notwithstanding their pretended conquest of the passions, yielded thus far to them. And the Epicureans, who indulged the pleasures of sense, to avoid its pains chose rather to put an end to it. This jailer thought there was no harm in anticipating his own death; but Christianity proves itself to be of God by this, that it keeps us to the law of our creation—revives, enforces, and establishes it, obliges us to be just to our own lives, and teaches us cheerfully to resign them to our graces, but courageously to hold them out against our corruptions. (4.) Paul stopped him from his proceeding against himself (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.28">v. 28</reference>): He <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice,</hi> not only to make him hear, but to make him heed, <hi type="italic">saying, Do not practise any evil to thyself; Do thyself no harm.</hi> All the cautions of the word of God against sin, and all appearances of it and approaches to it, have this tendency, "<hi type="italic">Do thyself no harm.</hi> Man, woman, do not wrong thyself, nor ruin thyself; hurt not thyself, and then none else can hurt thee; do not sin, for nothing else can hurt thee." Even as to the body, we are cautioned against those sins which do harm to it, and are taught to <hi type="italic">hate our own flesh, but to nourish and cherish it.</hi> The jailer needs not fear being called to an account for the escape of his prisoners, for <hi type="italic">they are all here.</hi> It was strange that some of them did not slip away, when the prison-doors were opened, and they were loosed from their bands; but their amazement held them fast, and, being sensible it was by the prayers of Paul and Silas that they were loosed, they would not stir unless they stirred; and God showed his power in binding their spirits, as much as in loosing their feet. <div eID="gen29751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29752" type="x-p"/> 2. He is afraid he shall lose his soul, and Paul makes him easy as to this care too. One concern leads him to another, and a much greater; and, being hindered from hastening himself out of this world, he begins to think, if he had pursued his intention, whither death would have brought him, and what would have become of him on the other side death—a very proper thought for such as have been snatched as a brand out of the fire, when there was but a step between them and death. Perhaps the heinousness of the sin he was running into helped to alarm him. <div eID="gen29752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29753" type="x-p"/> (1.) Whatever was the cause, he was put into a great consternation. The Spirit of God, that was sen to convince, in order to his being a Comforter, struck a terror upon him, and startled him. Whether he took care to shut the prison-doors again we are not told. Perhaps he forgot this as the woman of Samaria, when Christ had impressed convictions on her conscience, <hi type="italic">left her water-pot</hi> and forgot her errand to the well; for <hi type="italic">he called for a light</hi> with all speed, and <hi type="italic">sprang in</hi> to the inner prison, <hi type="italic">and came trembling to Paul and Silas.</hi> Those that have sin set in order before them, and are made to know their abominations, cannot but tremble at the apprehension of their misery and danger. This jailer, when he was thus made to tremble, could not apply to a more proper person than to Paul, for it had once been his own case; he had been once a persecutor of good men, as this jailer was—had cast them into prison, as he kept them—and when, like him, he was made sensible of it, <hi type="italic">he trembled, and was astonished;</hi> and therefore he was able to speak the more feelingly to the jailer. <div eID="gen29753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29754" type="x-p"/> (2.) In this consternation, he applied to Paul and Silas for relief. Observe, [1.] How reverent and respectful his address to them is: <hi type="italic">He called for a light,</hi> because they were in the dark, and that they might see what a fright he was in; <hi type="italic">he fell down before them,</hi> as one amazed at the badness of his own condition, and ready to sink under the load of his terror because of it; he fell down before them, as one that had upon his spirit an awe of them, and of the image of God upon them, and of their commission from God. It is probable that he had heard what the damsel said of them, that they were <hi type="italic">the servants of the living God, who showed to them the way of salvation,</hi> and as such he thus expressed his veneration for them. He fell down before them, to beg their pardon, as a penitent, for the indignities he had done them, and to beg their advice, as a supplicant, what he should do. He gave them a title of respect, <hi type="italic">Sirs,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kyrioi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">lords, masters;</hi> just now it was, <hi type="italic">Rogues</hi> and <hi type="italic">villains,</hi> and he was their master; but now, <hi type="italic">Sirs, lords,</hi> and they are his masters.
