Converting grace changes people's language of and to good people and good ministers; and, to such as are thoroughly convinced of sin, the very feet of those that bring tidings of Christ are beautiful; yea, though they are disgracefully fastened in the stocks. [2.] How serious his enquiry is: <hi type="italic">What must I do to be saved? First,</hi> His salvation is now his great concern, and lies nearest his heart, which before was the furthest thing from his thoughts. Not, What shall I do to be preferred, to be rich and great in the world? but, <hi type="italic">What shall I do to be saved? Secondly,</hi> He does not enquire concerning others, what they must do; but concerning himself, "What must I do?" It is his own precious soul that he is in care about: "Let others do as they please; tell me what I must do, what course I must take." <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He is convinced that something must be done, and done by him too, in order to his salvation: that it is not a thing of course, a thing that will do itself, but a thing about which we must strive, wrestle, and take pains. He asks not, "What may be done for me?" but, "What shall I do, that, being <hi type="italic">now in fear and trembling,</hi> I may <hi type="italic">work out my salvation?</hi>" as Paul speaks in his epistle to the church at Philippi, of which this jailer was, perhaps with respect to his trembling enquiry here, intimating that he must not only ask after salvation (as he had done), but <hi type="italic">work out his salvation with</hi> a holy <hi type="italic">trembling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Phil. ii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He is willing to do any thing: "Tell me what I must do, and I am here ready to do it. Sirs, put me into any way, if it be but the right way, and a sure way; though narrow, and thorny, and uphill, yet I will walk in it." Note, Those who are thoroughly convinced of sin, and truly concerned about their salvation, will surrender at discretion to Jesus Christ, will give him a blank to write what he pleases, will be glad to have Christ upon his own terms, Christ upon any terms. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> He is inquisitive what he should do, is desirous to know what he should do, and asks those that were likely to tell him. <hi type="italic">If you will enquire, enquire ye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Isa. xxi. 12</reference>. Those that set their faces Zionward must ask the way thither, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">Jer. l. 5</reference>. We cannot know it of ourselves, but God has made it known to us by his word, has appointed his ministers to assist us in consulting the scriptures, and has promised <hi type="italic">to give his Holy Spirit to those that ask him,</hi> to be their guide in the way of salvation. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> He <hi type="italic">brought them out,</hi> to put this question to them, that their answer might not be by duress or compulsion, but that they might prescribe to him, though he was their keeper, with the same liberty as they did to others. He brings them out of the dungeon, in hopes they will bring him out of a much worse. <div eID="gen29754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29755" type="x-p"/> (3.) They very readily directed him what he must do, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.31">v. 31</reference>. They were always ready to answer such enquiries; though they are cold, and sore, and sleepy, they do not adjourn this cause to a more convenient time and place, do not bid him come to them the next sabbath at their meeting-place by the river side, and they will tell him, but they strike while the iron is hot, take him now when he is in a good mind, lest the conviction should wear off. Now that God begins to work, it is time for them to set in as <hi type="italic">workers together with God.</hi> They do not upbraid him with his rude and ill carriage towards them, and his going beyond his warrant; all this is forgiven and forgotten, and they are as glad to show him the way to heaven as the best friend they have. They did not triumph over him, though he trembled; they gave him the same directions they did to others, <hi type="italic">Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> One would think they should have said, "Repent of thy abusing us, in the first place." No, that is overlooked and easily passed by, if he will but believe in Christ. This is an example to ministers to encourage penitents, to meet those that are coming to Christ and take them by the hand, not to be hard upon any for unkindness done to them, but to seek Christ's honour more than their own. Here is the sum of the whole gospel, the covenant of grace in a few words: <hi type="italic">Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.</hi> Here is, [1.] The happiness promised: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be saved;</hi> not only rescued from eternal ruin, but brought to eternal life and blessedness. Though thou art a <hi type="italic">poor man,</hi> an under-jailer or turnkey, mean and of low condition in the world, yet this shall be no bar to thy salvation. Though a great sinner, though a persecutor, yet thy heinous transgressions shall be all forgiven through the merits of Christ; and thy hard embittered heart shall be softened and sweetened by the grace of Christ, and thus thou shalt neither die for thy crime nor die of thy disease." [2.] The condition required: <hi type="italic">Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> We must admit the record that God hath given in his gospel concerning his Son, and assent to it as faithful, and well <hi type="italic">worthy of all acceptation.</hi> We must approve the method God has taken of reconciling the world to himself by a Mediator; and accept of Christ as he is offered to us, and give up ourselves to be ruled and taught and saved by him. This is the only way and a sure way to salvation. No other way of salvation than by Christ, and no other way of our being saved by Christ than by believing in him; and no danger of coming short if we take this way, for it is the way that God has appointed, and he is faithful that has promised. It is the gospel that is to be preached to every creature, <hi type="italic">He that believes shall be saved.</hi> [3.] The extension of this to his family: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be saved, and thy house;</hi> that is, "God will be in Christ a God to thee and to thy seed, as he was to Abraham. Believe, and salvation shall <hi type="italic">come to thy house,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Luke.19.9">Luke xix. 9</reference>. Those of thy house that are infants shall be admitted into the visible church with thee, and thereby put into a fair way for salvation; those that are grown up shall have the means of salvation brought to them, and, be they ever so many, let them believe in Jesus Christ and they shall be saved; they are all welcome to Christ upon the same terms." <div eID="gen29755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29756" type="x-p"/> (4.) They proceeded to instruct him and his family in the doctrine of Christ (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.32">v. 32</reference>): They <hi type="italic">spoke unto him the word of the Lord.</hi> He was, for aught that appears, an utter stranger to Christ, and therefore it is requisite he should be told who this Jesus is, that he may believe in him, <reference osisRef="John.9.36">John ix. 36</reference>. And, the substance of the matter lying in a little compass, they soon told him enough to make his being baptized a reasonable service. Christ's ministers should have the word of the Lord so ready to them, and so richly dwelling in them, as to be able to give instructions offhand to any that desire to hear and receive them, for their direction in the way of salvation. They spoke the word not only to him, but to <hi type="italic">all that were in his house.</hi> Masters of families should take care that all under their charge partake of the means of knowledge and grace, and that the word of the Lord be spoken to them; for the souls of the poorest servants are as precious as those of their masters, and are bought with the same price. <div eID="gen29756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29757" type="x-p"/> (5.) The jailer and his family were immediately baptized, and thereby took upon them the profession of Christianity, submitted to its laws, and were admitted to its privileges, upon their declaring solemnly, as the eunuch did, that they believed that <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ is the Son of God:</hi> He was <hi type="italic">baptized, he and all his, straightway.</hi> Neither he nor any of his family desired time to consider whether they should come into baptismal bonds or no; nor did Paul and Silas desire time to try their sincerity and to consider whether they should baptize them or no. But the Spirit of grace worked such a strong faith in them, all on a sudden, as superseded further debate; and Paul and Silas knew by the Spirit that it was a work of God that was wrought in them: so that there was no occasion for demur. This therefore will not justify such precipitation in ordinary cases. <div eID="gen29757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29758" type="x-p"/> (6.) The jailer was hereupon very respectful to Paul and Silas, as one that knew not how to make amends for the injury he had done to them, much less for the kindness he had received from them: He <hi type="italic">took them the same hour of the night,</hi> would not let them lie a minute longer in the inner prison; but, [1.] He <hi type="italic">washed their stripes,</hi> to cool them, and abate the smart of them; to clean them from the blood which the stripes had fetched. It is probable that he bathed them with some healing liquor, as the good Samaritan helped the wounded man by <hi type="italic">pouring in oil and wine.</hi> [2.] He <hi type="italic">brought them into his house,</hi> bade them welcome to the best room he had, and prepared his best bed for them. Now nothing was thought good enough for them, as before nothing bad enough. [3.] He <hi type="italic">set meat before them,</hi> such as his house would afford, and they were welcome to it, by which he expressed the welcome which his soul gave to the gospel. They had spoken to him the word of the Lord, had broken the bread of life to him and his family; and he, having reaped so plentifully of their spiritual things, thought it was but reasonable that they should reap of his carnal things, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1 Cor. ix. 11</reference>. What have we houses and tables for but as we have opportunity to serve God and his people with them? <div eID="gen29758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29759" type="x-p"/> (7.) The voice of rejoicing with that of salvation was heard in the jailer's house; never was such a truly merry night kept there before: <hi type="italic">He rejoiced, believing in God, with all his house.</hi> There was none in his house that refused to be baptized, and so made a jar in the harmony; but they were unanimous in embracing the gospel, which added much to the joy. Or it may be read, <hi type="italic">He, believing in God, rejoiced all the house over;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">panoiki</hi></hi>—he went to every apartment, expressing his joy. Observe, [1.] His believing in Christ is called believing <hi type="italic">in God,</hi> which intimates that Christ is God, and that the design of the gospel is so far from being to draw us from God (saying, <hi type="italic">Go serve other gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.13.2">Deut. xiii. 2</reference>) that it has a direct tendency to bring us to God. [2.] His faith produced joy. Those that by faith have given up themselves to God in Christ as theirs have a great deal of reason to rejoice. The eunuch, when he was converted, <hi type="italic">went on his way rejoicing;</hi> and here the jailer rejoiced. The conversion of the nations is spoken of in the Old Testament as their rejoicing, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">Ps. lxvii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">xcvi. 11</reference>. For, <hi type="italic">believing, we rejoice with joy unspeakable, and full of glory.</hi> Believing in Christ is rejoicing in Christ. [3.] He signified his joy to all about him. Out of the abundance of the joy in his heart, his mouth spoke to the glory of God, and their encouragement who believed in God too. Those who have themselves tasted the comforts of religion should do what they can to bring others to the taste of them. One cheerful Christian should make many.
entries.52e8f7ef03c8b7055870ad742d83a8bbb0dcd341: <div eID="gen29759" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul and Silas Released.</title> <div sID="gen29760" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And when it was day, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go. <hi type="super">36</hi> And the keeper of the prison told this saying to Paul, The magistrates have sent to let you go: now therefore depart, and go in peace. <hi type="super">37</hi> But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast <hi type="italic">us</hi> into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were <reference osisRef="Rom.39">Romans. 39</reference> And they came and besought them, and brought <hi type="italic">them</hi> out, and desired <hi type="italic">them</hi> to depart out of the city. 40 And they went out of the prison, and entered into <hi type="italic">the house of</hi> Lydia: and when they had seen the brethren, they comforted them, and departed. <div eID="gen29760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29761" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen29761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29762" type="x-p"/> I. Orders sent for the discharge of Paul and Silas out of prison <reference osisRef="Acts.16.35-Acts.16.36">v. 35, 36</reference>. 1. The magistrates that had so basely abused them the day before gave the orders; and their doing it so early, <hi type="italic">as soon as it was day,</hi> intimates that either they were sensible the terrific earthquake they felt at midnight was intended to plead the cause of their prisoners, or their consciences had smitten them for what they had done and made them very uneasy. While the persecuted were singing in the stocks, the persecutors were full of tossings to and fro upon their beds, through anguish of mind, complaining more of the lashes of their consciences than the prisoners did of the lashes on their backs, and more in haste to give them a discharge than they were to petition for one. Now God caused his servants to be <hi type="italic">pitied of those that had carried them captives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.46">Ps. cvi. 46</reference>. The magistrates sent <hi type="italic">sergeants,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">rabdouchous</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">those that had the rods,</hi> the vergers, the tipstaves, the beadles, those that had been employed in beating them, that they might go and ask them forgiveness. The order was, <hi type="italic">Let those men go.</hi> It is probable that they designed further mischief to them, but God turned their hearts, and, as he had made their wrath hitherto to praise him, so the remainder thereof he did restrain, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Ps. lxxvi. 10</reference>. 2. The jailer brought them the news (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">The magistrates have sent to let you go.</hi> Some think the jailer had betimes transmitted an account to the magistrates of what had passed in his house that night, and so had obtained this order for the discharge of his prisoners: <hi type="italic">Now therefore depart.</hi> Not that he was desirous to part with them as his guests, but as his prisoners; they shall still be welcome to his house, but he is glad they are at liberty from his stocks. God could by his grace as easily have converted the magistrates as the jailer, and have brought them to faith and baptism; but God hath <hi type="italic">chosen the poor of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">James ii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen29762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29763" type="x-p"/> II. Paul's insisting upon the breach of privilege which the magistrates had been guilty of, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.37">v. 37</reference>. Paul said to the sergeants, "<hi type="italic">They have beaten us openly, uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison</hi> against all law and justice, and <hi type="italic">now do they thrust us out privily,</hi> and think to make us amends with this for the injury done us? <hi type="italic">Nay, verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us our,</hi> and own that they have done us wrong." It is probable that the magistrates had some intimation that they were Romans, and were made sensible that their fury had carried them further than the law would bear them out; and that this was the reason why they gave orders for their discharge. Now observe, <div eID="gen29763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29764" type="x-p"/> 1. Paul did not plead this before he was beaten, though it is probable that it might have prevented it, lest he should seem to be afraid of suffering for the truth which he had preached. Tully, in one of his orations, against Verres, tells of one Ganius, who was ordered by Verres to be beaten in Sicily, that all the while he was under the lash he cried out nothing but <hi type="italic">Civis Romanus sum—I am a citizen of Rome;</hi> Paul did not do so; he had nobler things than this to comfort himself with in his affliction. <div eID="gen29764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29765" type="x-p"/> 2. He did plead it afterwards, to put an honour upon his sufferings and upon the cause he suffered for, to let the world know that the preachers of the gospel were not such despicable men as they were commonly looked upon to be, and that they merited better treatment. He did it likewise to mollify the magistrates towards the Christians at Philippi, and to gain better treatment for them, and beget in the people a better opinion of the Christian religion, when they saw that Paul had a fair advantage against their magistrates, might have brought his action against them and had them called to an account for what they had done, and yet did not take the advantage, which was very much to the honour of that worthy name by which he was called. Now here, <div eID="gen29765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29766" type="x-p"/> (1.) Paul lets them know how many ways they had run themselves into a premunire, and that he had law enough to know it. [1.] They had <hi type="italic">beaten</hi> those that were Romans; some think that Silas was a Roman citizen as well as Paul; others that this does not necessarily follow. Paul was a citizen, and Silas was his companion. Now both the <hi type="italic">lex Procia</hi> and the <hi type="italic">lex Sempronia</hi> did expressly forbid <hi type="italic">liberum corpus Romani civis, virgis aut aliis verberibus cædi—the free body of a Roman citizen to be beaten with rods or otherwise.</hi> Roman historians give instances of cities that had their charters taken from them for indignities done to Roman citizens; we shall afterwards find Paul making use of this plea, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.25-Acts.22.26">ch. xxii. 25, 26</reference>. To tell them they had beaten those who were the messengers of Christ and the favourites of Heaven would have had no influence upon them; but to tell them they have abused Roman citizens will put them into a fright: so common is it for people to be more afraid of Cæsar's wrath than of Christ's. He that affronts a Roman, a gentleman, a nobleman, though ignorantly, and through mistake, thinks himself concerned to cry <hi type="italic">Peccavi—I have done wrong,</hi> and make his submission; but he that persecutes a Christian because he belongs to Christ stands to it, and thinks he may do it securely, though God hath said, <hi type="italic">He that toucheth them toucheth the apple of my eye,</hi> and Christ has warned us of the danger of <hi type="italic">offending his little ones.</hi> [2.] They had beaten them <hi type="italic">uncondemned; indicta causa—without a fair hearing,</hi> had not calmly examined what was said against them, much less enquired what they had to say for themselves. It is a universal rule of justice, <hi type="italic">Caus&#226; cognit&#226; possunt multi absolvi, incognit&#226; nemo condemnari potest—Many may be acquitted in consequence of having had a hearing, while without a hearing no one can be condemned.</hi> Christ's servants would not have been abused as they have been if they and their cause might but have had an impartial trial. [3.] It was an aggravation of this that they had done it openly, which, as it was so much the greater disgrace to the sufferers, so it was the bolder defiance to justice and the law. [4.] They had <hi type="italic">cast them into prison,</hi> without showing any cause of their commitment, and in an arbitrary manner, by a verbal order. [5.] They now <hi type="italic">thrust them out privily;</hi> they had not indeed the impudence to stand by what they had done, but yet had not the honesty to own themselves in a fault. <div eID="gen29766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29767" type="x-p"/> (2.) He insists upon it that they should make them an acknowledgment of their error, and give them a public discharge, to make it the more honourable, as they had done them a public disgrace, which made that the more disgraceful: "<hi type="italic">Let them come themselves, and fetch us out,</hi> and give a testimony to our innocency, and that we have done nothing worthy of stripes or of bonds." It was not a point of honour that Paul stood thus stiffly upon, but a point of justice, and not to himself so much as to his cause: "Let them come and stop the clamours of the people, by confessing that we are not the troublers of the city." <div eID="gen29767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29768" type="x-p"/> III. The magistrates' submission, and the reversing of the judgment given against Paul and Silas, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.38-Acts.16.39">v. 38, 39</reference>. 1. The magistrates were frightened when they were told (though it may be they knew it before) that Paul was a Roman. They feared when they heard it, lest some of his friends should inform the government of what they had done, and they should fare the worse for it. The proceedings of persecutors have often been illegal, even by the law of nations, and often inhuman, against the law of nature, but always sinful, and against God's law. 2. They <hi type="italic">came and besought them</hi> not to take advantage of the law against them, but to overlook the illegality of what they had done and say no more of it: they <hi type="italic">brought them out</hi> of the prison, owning that they were wrongfully put into it, and desired them that they would peaceably and quietly <hi type="italic">depart out of the city.</hi> Thus Pharaoh and his servants, who had set God and Moses at defiance, came to Moses, and <hi type="italic">bowed down themselves to him, saying, Get thee out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.11.8">Exod. xi. 8</reference>. God can make the enemies of his people ashamed of their envy and enmity to them, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. Jerusalem is sometimes made a burdensome stone to those that heave at it, which they would gladly get clear of, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">Zech. xii. 3</reference>. Yet, if the repentance of these magistrates had been sincere, they would not have desired them to depart out of their city (as the Gadarenes desired to be rid of Christ), but would have courted their stay, and begged of them to continue in their city, to show them the way of salvation. But many are convinced that Christianity is not to be persecuted who yet are not convinced that it ought to be embraced, or at least are not persuaded to embrace it. They are compelled to do honour to Christ and his servants, <hi type="italic">to worship before their feet, and to know that he has loved them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>), and yet do not go so far as to have benefit by Christ, or to come in for a share in his love. <div eID="gen29768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29769" type="x-p"/> IV. The departure of Paul and Silas from Philippi, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.40">v. 40</reference>. They went out of the prison when they were legally discharged, and not till then, though they were illegally committed, and then, 1. They took leave of their friends: they <hi type="italic">went to the house of Lydia,</hi> where probably the disciples had met to pray for them, and there they <hi type="italic">saw the brethren,</hi> or visited them at their respective habitations (which was soon done, they were so few); and they <hi type="italic">comforted them,</hi> by telling them (saith an ancient Greek commentary) what God had done for them, and how he had owned them in the prison. They encouraged them to keep close to Christ, and hold fast the profession of their faith, whatever difficulties they might meet with, assuring them that all would then end well, everlastingly well. Young converts should have a great deal said to them to comfort them, for <hi type="italic">the joy of the Lord will be</hi> very much <hi type="italic">their strength.</hi> 2. They quitted the town: <hi type="italic">They departed.</hi> I wonder they should do so; for, now that they had had such an honourable discharge from their imprisonment, surely they might have gone on at least for some time in their work without danger; but I suppose they went away upon that principle of their Master's (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.38">Mark i. 38</reference>). <hi type="italic">Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also, for therefore came I forth.</hi> Paul and Silas had an extraordinary call to Philippi; and yet, when they have come thither, they see little of the fruit of their labours, and are soon driven thence. Yet they did not come in vain. Though the beginnings here were <hi type="italic">small, the latter end greatly increased;</hi> now they laid the foundation of a church at Philippi, which became very eminent, had its bishops and deacons, and people that were more generous to Paul than any other church, as appears by his epistle to the Philippians, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.25">iv. 25</reference>. Let not ministers be discouraged, though they see not the fruit of their labours presently; the seed sown seems to be lost under the clods, but it shall come up again in a plentiful harvest in due time.  <chapter eID="Acts.16"/> <div eID="gen29769" type="x-p"/>

entries.fb76b2325a289b87696ad158971eb1cde76b33c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15958"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <div sID="gen30760" type="x-p"/> PAUL'S SECOND MISSIONARY JOURNEY. Ac 15:41-18:22.<div eID="gen30760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30761" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.41-Acts.16.5">Ac 15:41-16:5</reference>. Visitation of the Churches Formerly Established, Timotheus Here Joining the Missionary Party.<div eID="gen30761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">41. he went through Syria and Cilicia--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.15.23">Ac 15:23</reference>). Taking probably the same route as when despatched in haste from Jerusalem to Tarsus, he then went by land (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.9.30">Ac 9:30</reference>).<div eID="gen30762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15958"/><hi type="bold">1-5. Then came he to Derbe and Lystra; and, behold, a certain disciple was there--</hi>that is, at Lystra (not Derbe, as some conclude from <reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>).<div eID="gen30763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">named Timotheus--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.14.20">Ac 14:20</reference>). As Paul styles him "his own son in the faith" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>), he must have been gained to Christ at the apostle's first visit; and as Paul says he "had fully known his persecutions which came on him at Lystra" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10">2Ti 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.11">11</reference>), he may have been in that group of disciples that surrounded the apparently lifeless body of the apostle outside the walls of Lystra, and that at a time of life when the mind receives its deepest impressions from the spectacle of innocent suffering and undaunted courage [Howson]. His would be one of "the souls of the disciples confirmed" at the apostle's second visit, "exhorted to continue in the faith, and" warned "that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.21">Ac 14:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen30764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the son of a certain ... Jewess--</hi>"The unfeigned faith which dwelt first in his grandmother Lois" descended to "his mother Eunice," and thence it passed to this youth (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>), who "from a child knew the Holy Scriptures" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>). His gifts and destination to the ministry of Christ had already been attested (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">4:14</reference>); and though some ten years after this Paul speaks of him as still young (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>), "he was already well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium" (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.2">Ac 16:2</reference>), and consequently must have been well known through all that quarter.<div eID="gen30765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but his father was a Greek--</hi>Such mixed marriages, though little practiced, and disliked by the stricter Jews in Palestine, must have been very frequent among the Jews of the dispersion, especially in remote districts, where but few of the scattered people were settled [Howson]. <div eID="gen30766" type="x-p"/>
entries.389e2e25d7e0f22e74155ac17f7677da3e15c689: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15961"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.16.6-Acts.16.12">Ac 16:6-12</reference>. They Break New Ground in Phrygia and Galatia--Their Course in That Direction Being Mysteriously Hedged Up, They Travel Westward to Troas, Where They Are Divinely Directed to Macedonia--The Historian Himself Here Joining the Missionary Party, They Embark for Neapolis, and Reach Philippi.</title> <div sID="gen30771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15961"/><hi type="bold">6-8. Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia--</hi>proceeding in a northwesterly direction. At this time must have been formed "the churches of Galatia" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.2">Ga 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.1">1Co 16:1</reference>); founded, as we learn from the Epistle to the Galatians (particularly <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>), by the apostle Paul, and which were already in existence when he was on his third missionary journey, as we learn from <reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>, where it appears that he was no less successful in Phrygia. Why these proceedings, so interesting as we should suppose, are not here detailed, it is not easy to say; for the various reasons suggested are not very satisfactory: for example, that the historian had not joined the party [Alford]; that he was in haste to bring the apostle to Europe [Olshausen]; that the main stream of the Church's development was from Jerusalem to Rome, and the apostle's labors in Phrygia and Galatia lay quite out of the line of that direction [Baumgarten].<div eID="gen30771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost--</hi>speaking by some prophet, see on <reference osisRef="Acts.11.27">Ac 11:27</reference>.<div eID="gen30772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to preach the word in Asia--</hi>not the great Asiatic continent, nor even the rich peninsula now called Asia Minor, but only so much of its western coast as constituted the Roman province of Asia. <div eID="gen30773" type="x-p"/>
entries.06b6be364aeed81bfc850ef60199a6c4155d9eea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15964"/><div sID="gen30781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15964"/><hi type="bold">9-10. a vision appeared to Paul in the night--</hi>while awake, for it is not called a dream.<div eID="gen30781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us--</hi>Stretching his eye across the Ægean Sea, from Troas on the northeast, to the Macedonian hills, visible on the northwest, the apostle could hardly fail to think this the destined scene of his future labors; and, if he retired to rest with this thought, he would be thoroughly prepared for the remarkable intimation of the divine will now to be given him. This visional Macedonian discovered himself by what he said. But it was a cry not of conscious desire for the Gospel, but of deep need of it and unconscious preparedness to receive it, not only in that region, but, we may well say, throughout all that western empire which Macedonia might be said to represent. It was a virtual confession "that the highest splendor of heathendom, which we must recognize in the arts of Greece and in the polity and imperial power of Rome, had arrived at the end of all its resources. God had left the Gentile peoples to walk in their own ways (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.2">Ac 14:2</reference>). They had sought to gain salvation for themselves; but those who had carried it farthest along the paths of natural development were now pervaded by the feeling that all had indeed been vanity. This feeling is the simple, pure result of all the history of heathendom. And Israel, going along the way which God had marked out for him, had likewise arrived at his end. At last he is in a condition to realize his original vocation, by becoming the guide who is to lead the Gentiles unto God, the only Author and Creator of man's redemption; and Paul is in truth the very person in whom this vocation of Israel is now a present divine reality, and to whom, by this nocturnal apparition of the Macedonian, the preparedness of the heathen world to receive the ministry of Israel towards the Gentiles is confirmed" [Baumgarten]. This voice cries from heathendom still to the Christian Church, and never does the Church undertake the work of missions, nor any missionary go forth from it, in the right spirit, save in obedience to this cry. <div eID="gen30782" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c9a204fcdf3f8dc0ace035372ff9b4429ddd9b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15966"/><div sID="gen30784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15966"/><hi type="bold">11-12. Therefore loosing from Troas, we came--</hi>literally, "ran."<div eID="gen30784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a straight course--</hi>that is, "ran before the wind."<div eID="gen30785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to Samothracia--</hi>a lofty island on the Thracian coast, north from Troas, with an inclination westward. The wind must have set in strong from the south or south-southeast to bring them there so soon, as the current is strong in the opposite direction, and they afterwards took five days to what they now did in two (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">Ac 20:6</reference>) [Howson].<div eID="gen30786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">next day to Neapolis--</hi>on the Macedonian, or rather Thracian, coast, about sixty-five miles from Samothracia, and ten from Philippi, of which it is the harbor. <div eID="gen30787" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9019159726ed1e4e508c35650dfc8299c00789a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15970"/><div sID="gen30797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15970"/><hi type="bold">14-15. Lydia--</hi>a common name among the Greeks and Romans.<div eID="gen30797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira--</hi>on the confines of Lydia and Phrygia. The Lydians, particularly the inhabitants of Thyatira, were celebrated for their dyeing, in which they inherited the reputation of the Tyrians. Inscriptions to this effect, yet remaining, confirm the accuracy of our historian. This woman appears to have been in good circumstances, having an establishment at Philippi large enough to accommodate the missionary party (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.15">Ac 16:15</reference>), and receiving her goods from her native town.<div eID="gen30798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which worshipped God--</hi>that is, was a proselyte to the Jewish faith, and as such present at this meeting.<div eID="gen30799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose heart the Lord opened--</hi>that is, the Lord Jesus (see <reference osisRef="Acts.16.15">Ac 16:15</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="Luke.24.45">Lu 24:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Mt 11:27</reference>).<div eID="gen30800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that she attended to the things ... spoken by Paul--</hi>"showing that the inclination of the heart towards the truth originates not in the will of man. The first disposition to turn to the Gospel is a work of grace" [Olshausen]. Observe here the place assigned to "giving attention" or "heed" to the truth--that species of attention which consists in having the whole mind engrossed with it, and in apprehending and drinking it in, in its vital and saving character. <div eID="gen30801" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1ac832a88e4debfa6a7fe9b00f888cb30dcbeec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15972"/><div sID="gen30805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15972"/><hi type="bold">16-18. as we went to prayer--</hi>The words imply that it was on their way to the usual place of public prayer, by the river-side, that this took place; therefore not on the same day with what had just occurred.<div eID="gen30805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a ... damsel--</hi>a female servant, and in this case a slave (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.19">Ac 16:19</reference>).<div eID="gen30806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">possessed of a spirit of divination--</hi>or, of Python, that is, a spirit supposed to be inspired by the Pythian Apollo, or of the same nature. The reality of this demoniacal possession is as undeniable as that of any in the Gospel history. <div eID="gen30807" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b2748396901516f30c4ff405e6c7c9f88846e8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15975"/><div sID="gen30811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15975"/><hi type="bold">19. when her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone, they caught Paul and Silas--</hi>as the leading persons.<div eID="gen30811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and drew them into the market-place--</hi>or Forum, where the courts were.<div eID="gen30812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the magistrates, saying, &c.--</hi>We have here a full and independent confirmation of the reality of this supernatural cure, since on any other supposition such conduct would be senseless. <div eID="gen30813" type="x-p"/>
entries.e11edd543e0cc73a394ec500c7bffdd2963b1443: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15976"/><div sID="gen30814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15976"/><hi type="bold">20. These men, being Jews--</hi>objects of dislike, contempt, and suspicion by the Romans, and at this time of more than usual prejudice.<div eID="gen30814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do exceedingly trouble our city--</hi>See similar charges, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Ac 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.5">24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">1Ki 18:17</reference>. There is some color of truth in all such accusations, in so far as the Gospel, and generally the fear of God, as a reigning principle of human action, is in a godless world a thoroughly revolutionary principle ... How far external commotion and change will in any case attend the triumph of this principle depends on the breadth and obstinacy of the resistance it meets with. <div eID="gen30815" type="x-p"/>
entries.6307626a56cf0c7df5b5f26701191280bad29ed7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15977"/><div sID="gen30816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15977"/><hi type="bold">21. And teach customs, which are not lawful for us to receive, neither to observe, being Romans--</hi>Here also there was a measure of truth; as the introduction of new gods was forbidden by the laws, and this might be thought to apply to any change of religion. But the whole charge was pure hypocrisy; for as these men would have let the missionaries preach what religion they pleased if they had not dried up the source of their gains, so they conceal the real cause of their rage under color of a zeal for religion, and law, and good order: so <reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Ac 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.25">19:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.27">27</reference>. <div eID="gen30816" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8e570f7ae3939fd225c48cb3f3ab2d46afe41f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15978"/><div sID="gen30817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15978"/><hi type="bold">22. the multitude rose up together against them--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Acts.19.28">Ac 19:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.30">21:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.18">Lu 23:18</reference>.<div eID="gen30817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the magistrates rent off their--</hi>Paul's and Silas'<div eID="gen30818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clothes--</hi>that is, ordered the lictors, or rod-bearers, to tear them off, so as to expose their naked bodies (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.37">Ac 16:37</reference>). The word expresses the roughness with which this was done to prisoners preparatory to whipping.<div eID="gen30819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and commanded to beat them--</hi>without any trial (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.37">Ac 16:37</reference>), to appease the popular rage. Thrice, it seems, Paul endured this indignity (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.25">2Co 11:25</reference>). <div eID="gen30820" type="x-p"/>
entries.69d97971865935fd17aa52f65977dd39a780b7af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15979"/><div sID="gen30821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15979"/><hi type="bold">23-24. when they had laid many stripes upon them--</hi>the bleeding wounds from which they were not washed till it was done by the converted jailer (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.33">Ac 16:33</reference>).<div eID="gen30821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charged the jailer ... who ... thrust them into the inner prison--</hi>"pestilential cells, damp and cold, from which the light was excluded, and where the chains rusted on the prisoners. One such place may be seen to this day on the slope of the Capitol at Rome" [Howson]. <div eID="gen30822" type="x-p"/>
entries.906c9d9e403d41b9dd3bf52f556a8fcf4c9a8185: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15981"/><div sID="gen30824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15981"/><hi type="bold">25. And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises--</hi>literally, "praying, were singing praises"; that is, while engaged in pouring out their hearts in prayer, had broken forth into singing, and were hymning loud their joy. As the word here employed is that used to denote the Paschal hymn sung by our Lord and His disciples after their last Passover (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.30">Mt 26:30</reference>), and which we know to have consisted of Psa 113:1-118:29, which was chanted at that festival, it is probable that it was portions of the Psalms, so rich in such matter, which our joyous sufferers chanted forth; nor could any be more seasonable and inspiring to them than those very six Psalms, which every devout Jew would no doubt know by heart. "He giveth songs in the night" (<reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference>). Though their bodies were still bleeding and tortured in the stocks, their spirits, under "the expulsive power of a new affection," rose above suffering, and made the prison wails resound with their song. "In these midnight hymns, by the imprisoned witnesses for Jesus Christ, the whole might of Roman injustice and violence against the Church is not only set at naught, but converted into a foil to set forth more completely the majesty and spiritual power of the Church, which as yet the world knew nothing of. And if the sufferings of these two witnesses of Christ are the beginning and the type of numberless martyrdoms which were to flow upon the Church from the same source, in like manner the unparalleled triumph of the Spirit over suffering was the beginning and the pledge of a spiritual power which we afterwards see shining forth so triumphantly and irresistibly in the many martyrs of Christ who were given up as a prey to the same imperial might of Rome" [Neander in Baumgarten].<div eID="gen30824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the prisoners heard them--</hi>literally, "were listening to them," that is, when the astounding events immediately to be related took place; not asleep, but wide awake and rapt (no doubt) in wonder at what they heard. <div eID="gen30825" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a727aecac5f50cef495e8b7cba7c0824ac2f61f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15982"/><div sID="gen30826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15982"/><hi type="bold">26-28. And suddenly there was a great earthquake--</hi>in answer, doubtless, to the prayers and expectations of the sufferers that, for the truth's sake and the honor of their Lord, some interposition would take place.<div eID="gen30826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one's bands--</hi>that is, the bands of all the prisoners.<div eID="gen30827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were loosed--</hi>not by the earthquake, of course, but by a miraculous energy accompanying it. By this and the joyous strains which they had heard from the sufferers, not to speak of the change wrought on the jailer, these prisoners could hardly fail to have their hearts in some measure opened to the truth; and this part of the narrative seems the result of information afterwards communicated by one or more of these men. <div eID="gen30828" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fc91c38669a9ce295ad184583cafd1d85579064: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15985"/><div sID="gen30832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15985"/><hi type="bold">29-30. Then he called for a light, and sprang in ... and fell down before Paul and Silas, and brought them out and said--</hi>How graphic this rapid succession of minute details, evidently from the parties themselves, the prisoners and the jailer, who would talk over every feature of the scene once and again, in which the hand of the Lord had been so marvellously seen. <div eID="gen30832" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fae6be2747eab8796aa56b7e3a98c8e15b26add: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15987"/><div sID="gen30834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15987"/><hi type="bold">31-34. Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved--</hi>The brevity, simplicity, and directness of this reply are, in the circumstances, singularly beautiful. Enough at that moment to have his faith directed simply to the Saviour, with the assurance that this would bring to his soul the needed and sought salvation--the how being a matter for after teaching.<div eID="gen30834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt be saved, and thy house--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.10">Lu 19:10</reference>). <div eID="gen30835" type="x-p"/>
entries.547aa2b9b481a7f50aa8d742a339bbffd28a3449: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15991"/><div sID="gen30844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15991"/><hi type="bold">35-36. when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, Let those men go--</hi>The cause of this change can only be conjectured. When the commotion ceased, reflection would soon convince them of the injustice they had done, even supposing the prisoners had been entitled to no special privileges; and if rumor reached them that the prisoners were somehow under supernatural protection, they might be the more awed into a desire to get rid of them. <div eID="gen30844" type="x-p"/>
entries.cee947a7f32b2e7edfa76af0dc3e663d57a5a410: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15993"/><div sID="gen30847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15993"/><hi type="bold">37. Paul said unto them--</hi>to the sergeants who had entered the prison along with the jailer, that they might be able to report that the men had departed.<div eID="gen30847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They have beaten us openly--</hi>The publicity of the injury done them, exposing their naked and bleeding bodies to the rude populace, was evidently the most stinging feature of it to the apostle's delicate feeling, and to this accordingly he alludes to the Thessalonians, probably a year after: "Even after we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated (or 'insulted') as ye know at Philippi" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1Th 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen30848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncondemned--</hi>unconvicted on trial.<div eID="gen30849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being Romans--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.22.28">Ac 22:28</reference>).<div eID="gen30850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and cast us into prison--</hi>both illegal. Of Silas' citizenship, if meant to be included, we know nothing.<div eID="gen30851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and now do they thrust us out--</hi>hurry us out--see <reference osisRef="Mark.9.38">Mr 9:38</reference>, Greek.<div eID="gen30852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">privily?--</hi>Mark the intended contrast between the public insult they had inflicted and the private way in which they ordered them to be off.<div eID="gen30853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nay verily--</hi>no, indeed.<div eID="gen30854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but let them come themselves and fetch us out--</hi>by open and formal act, equivalent to a public declaration of their innocence. <div eID="gen30855" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1bacfd8e8d2dde599158da7d53fe8a63e55da57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15994"/><div sID="gen30856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15994"/><hi type="bold">38. they feared when they heard they were Romans--</hi>their authority being thus imperilled; for they were liable to an action for what they had done. <div eID="gen30856" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb951a744de227dc740c30cfbd9b332a4e7e6e3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15995"/><div sID="gen30857" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15995"/><hi type="bold">39-40. And they came--</hi>in person.<div eID="gen30857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and besought them--</hi>not to complain of them. What a contrast this suppliant attitude of the preachers of Philippi to the tyrannical air with which they had the day before treated the preachers! (See <reference osisRef="Isa.60.14">Is 60:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Re 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen30858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought them out--</hi>conducted them forth from the prison into the street, as insisted on.<div eID="gen30859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and desired--</hi>"requested."<div eID="gen30860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them to depart out of the city--</hi>perhaps fearing again to excite the populace. <div eID="gen30861" type="x-p"/>

entries.56e3d8aba1f2f432b8caef3a8e64ec5ab7572b5e: <div eID="gen44730" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen44731" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen44732" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen44732" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen44731" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen44733" type="x-p"/> Paul, coming to Derbe and Lystra, meets with Timothy, the son of a Jewess by a Greek father, whom he circumcises and takes with him into his work, <reference osisRef="Act.16.1-Act.16.3">Act 16:1-3</reference>. As they pass through the different cities, they deliver the apostles' decrees to the Churches; and they are established in the faith, and daily increase in numbers, <reference osisRef="Act.16.4">Act 16:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.5">Act 16:5</reference>. They travel through Phrygia, Galatia, Mysia, and to Troas, <reference osisRef="Act.16.6-Act.16.8">Act 16:6-8</reference>. Where Paul has a vision, relative to his preaching in Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.16.9">Act 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.10">Act 16:10</reference>. Leaving Troas, he sails to Samothracia and Neapolis, and comes to Philippi in Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.16.11">Act 16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.12">Act 16:12</reference>. Lydia, a seller of purple, receives the apostles teaching; and she and her family are baptized, <reference osisRef="Act.16.13-Act.16.16">Act 16:13-16</reference>. A young woman, with a spirit of divination, dispossessed by St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Act.16.16-Act.16.18">Act 16:16-18</reference>. Her masters, finding their gain by her soothsaying gone, make an attack upon Paul and Silas, drag them before the magistrates, who command them to be beaten, thrust into the closest prison, and their feet made fast in the stocks, <reference osisRef="Act.16.19-Act.16.24">Act 16:19-24</reference>. Paul and Silas singing praises at midnight, the prison doors are miraculously opened, and all the bonds of the prisoners loosed, <reference osisRef="Act.16.25">Act 16:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.26">Act 16:26</reference>. The keeper being alarmed, supposing that the prisoners were fled, is about to kill himself, but is prevented by Paul, <reference osisRef="Act.16.27-Act.16.28">Act 16:27-28</reference>. He inquires the way of salvation, believes, and he and his whole family are baptized, <reference osisRef="Act.16.29-Act.16.34">Act 16:29-34</reference>. The next morning the magistrates order the apostles to be dismissed, <reference osisRef="Act.16.35">Act 16:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.36">Act 16:36</reference>. Paul pleads his privilege as a Roman, and accuses the magistrates of injustice, who, being alarmed, come themselves to the prison, deliver them, and beg them to depart from the city, <reference osisRef="Act.16.37-Act.16.39">Act 16:37-39</reference>. They leave the prison, enter into the house of Lydia, comfort the brethren, and depart, <reference osisRef="Act.16.40">Act 16:40</reference>. <div eID="gen44733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44734" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen44734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44735" type="x-p"/> A certain disciple - Bishop Pearce would read the latter part of this verse and the beginning of the next thus - A certain disciple named Timotheus, (the son of a certain Jewish woman that believed, but of a father who was a Greek), who was well reported of by the brethren, etc. <div eID="gen44735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44736" type="x-p"/> This Timothy was the same person to whom St. Paul wrote those two noble epistles which are still extant. His mother's name was Eunice, as we learn from <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Tim 1:5</reference>. What his father's name was we know not; he was either a mere heathen, or, at most, only a proselyte of the gate, who never submitted to circumcision: had he submitted to this rite, he would, no doubt, have circumcised his son; but the son being without it is a proof that the father was so too. Some MSS. state that Timothy's mother was now a widow; but this does not appear to be well founded.
entries.c4fa34a798b3313f5b51a0805acaeebfba97be1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen44736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44737" type="x-p"/> Which was well reported of - These words are spoken of Timothy, and not of his father. At this time Timothy must have been very young; for, several years after, when appointed to superintend the Church at Crete, he appears to have been then so young that there was a danger of its operating to the prejudice of his ministry: <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Tim 4:12</reference>, Let no man despise thy youth. He had a very early religious education from his godly mother Eunice, and his not less pious grandmother Lois; and, from his religious instructions, was well prepared for the work to which God now called him.
entries.f37b12404ccc51dda6c0dd23f985ed6660fa9edc: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen44737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44738" type="x-p"/> Took and circumcised him - For this simple reason, that the Jews would neither have heard him preach, nor would have any connection with him, had he been otherwise. Besides, St. Paul himself could have had no access to the Jews in any place, had they known that he associated with a person who was uncircumcised: they would have considered both to be unclean. The circumcision of Timothy was a merely prudential regulation; one rendered imperiously necessary by the circumstances in which they were then placed; and, as it was done merely in reference to this, Timothy was lain under no necessity to observe the Mosaic ritual, nor could it prejudice his spiritual state, because he did not do it in order to seek justification by the law, for this he had before, through the faith of Christ. In <reference osisRef="Gal.2.3-Gal.2.5">Gal 2:3-5</reference>, we read that Paul refuses to circumcise Titus, who was a Greek, and his parents Gentiles, notwithstanding the entreaties of some zealous Judaizing Christians, as their object was to bring him under the yoke of the law: here, the case was widely different, and the necessity of the measure indisputable.
entries.7d31c52be597518c5ee6d2f29426a29e700fc741: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen44738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44739" type="x-p"/> They delivered them the decrees for to keep - Τα δογματα, τα κεκριμενα ὑπο των ΑποϚολων. Bishop Pearce contends that τα δογματα, the decrees, is a gloss which was not in the text originally; and that the τα κεκριμενα, the judgments or determinations of the apostles, was all that was originally written here. He supports his opinion by a reference to the word κρινω, I judge, used by James, <reference osisRef="Act.15.19">Act 15:19</reference>, whence the whole decision, as it referred - <div eID="gen44739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44740" type="x-p"/> 1. to the inexpediency of circumcising the Gentiles; and, <div eID="gen44740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44741" type="x-p"/> 2. to the necessity of observing the four precepts laid down, was called τα κεκριμενα, the things that were judged, or decided on; the judgments of the apostolic council. <div eID="gen44741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44742" type="x-p"/> Instead of κεκριμενα, the Syrian has a word that answers to γεγραμμενα, the decrees that were written. The word δογμα, from δοκεω, to think proper, determine, decree, signifies an ordinance or decree, properly and deliberately made, relative to any important point, and which, in reference to that point, has the force of law. Our term dogma, which we often abuse, is the Greek word in English letters.
entries.7e3538fbad8c1b5360b62625a6352c6fb946e468: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen44742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44743" type="x-p"/> And so were the Churches established - The disputations at Antioch, relative to circumcision, had no doubt spread far and wide among other Churches, and unhinged many. The decrees of the apostles came in good time, and prevented farther mischief: the people, saved from uncertainty, became established in the faith; and the Church had a daily accession of converted souls.
entries.c7672613df008f4bc6789d50b20efbbbacf865de: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen44743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44744" type="x-p"/> Were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia - The Asia mentioned here could not be Asia Minor in general, for Galatia, Phrygia, Pisidia, Lycaonia, and Pamphylia, were provinces of it, and in these the apostles preached; but it was what was called Proconsular Asia, which included only Ionia, Aeolia, and Lydia. The apostles were not suffered to visit these places at this time; but they afterwards went thither, and preached the Gospel with success; for it was in this Proconsular Asia that the seven Churches were situated. God chose to send his servants to another place, where he saw that the word would be affectionately received; and probably those in Proconsular Asia were not, as yet, sufficiently prepared to receive and profit by it.
entries.ae41e305f0addbad6bbacc9c8de8c0e8f7093cb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen44744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44745" type="x-p"/> After they were come to Mysia - They passed through Phrygia into Mysia, which lay between Bithynia on the north, Phrygia on the east, Aeolia on the south, and the Mediterranean on the west. <div eID="gen44745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44746" type="x-p"/> But the Spirit suffered them not - God saw that that was not the most proper time to preach the word at Bithynia; as he willed them to go immediately to Macedonia, the people there being ripe for the word of life. Instead of το πνευμα, the Spirit merely, το πνευμα Ιησου, the Spirit of Jesus, is the reading of ABCDE, several others, with both the Syriac, the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate, Itala, and several of the fathers. The reading is undoubtedly genuine, and should be immediately restored to the text.
entries.a5b49c76f89427c6c71d70e49b064fb7a7b8abec: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen44746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44747" type="x-p"/> Came down to Troas - The Troad, or part of Phrygia Minor in which the celebrated city of Troy was formerly situated. This city was first built by Dardanus, who was its king, and from whom it was called Dardania; from Tros, his grandson, it was called Troja, or Troy; and from his son, Ilus, it was called Ilium. It has been long so completely destroyed that no ascertainable vestige of it remains; insomuch that some have even doubted of its existence. Those who contend for the reality of the history of Troy suppose it to have stood on the site of the modern village Bounarbachi, about twelve miles from the sea, on an eminence, at the termination of a spacious plain.
entries.a055041a2989dfbcb2b99f2c9dfe14686f434fd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen44747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44748" type="x-p"/> A vision appeared to Paul in the night - Whether this was in a dream, or whether a representation made to the senses of the apostle, we cannot tell. A man of Macedonia appeared to him, and made this simple communication, Come over into Macedonia, and help us. <div eID="gen44748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44749" type="x-p"/> Some suppose that the guardian angel of Macedonia appeared to St. Paul in a human shape; others, that it was a Divine communication made to his imagination in a dream.
entries.0c18b6706524cdf7fee5c7d6a3c8fbac7970f1ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen44749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44750" type="x-p"/> We endeavored to go into Macedonia - This is the first place that the historian St. Luke refers to himself: We endeavored, etc. And, from this, it has been supposed that he joined the company of Paul, for the first time, at Troas. <div eID="gen44750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44751" type="x-p"/> Assuredly gathering - Συμβιβαζοντες, Drawing an inference from the vision that had appeared. <div eID="gen44751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44752" type="x-p"/> That the Lord had called us for to preach - That is, they inferred that they were called to preach the Gospel in Macedonia, from what the vision had said, come over and help us; the help meaning, preach to us the Gospel. Instead of ὁ Κυριος, the Lord, meaning Jesus, several MSS., such as ABCE, several others, with the Coptic, Vulgate, Theophylact, and Jerome, have ὁ Θεος, God. Though this stands on very reputable authority, yet the former seems to be the better reading; for it was the Spirit of Jesus, <reference osisRef="Act.16.7">Act 16:7</reference>, that would not suffer them to go into Bithynia, because he had designed that they should immediately preach the Gospel in Macedonia.
entries.aeadcd0123575887a9f22e8ce09844137a16e13f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen44752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44753" type="x-p"/> Loosing from Troas - Setting sail from this place. <div eID="gen44753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44754" type="x-p"/> With a straight course to Samothracia - This was an island of the Aegean Sea, contiguous to Thrace, and hence called Samothracia, or the Thracian Samos. It is about twenty miles in circumference, and is now called Samandrachi by the Turks, who are its present masters. <div eID="gen44754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44755" type="x-p"/> And the next day to Neapolis - There were many cities of this name; but this was a sea-port town of Macedonia, a few miles eastward of Philippi. Neapolis signifies the new city.
entries.c20e3ab5a0e909e4db2af1978f2905388c4fcef6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen44755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44756" type="x-p"/> And from thence to Philippi - This was a town of Macedonia, in the territory of the Edones, on the confines of Thrace, situated on the side of a steep eminence. It took its name from Philip II., king of Macedon. It is famous for two battles, fought between the imperial army, commanded by Octavianus, afterwards Augustus, and Mark Antony, and the republican army, commanded by Brutus and Cassius, in which these were successful; and a second, between Octavianus and Antony on the one part, and Brutus on the other. In this battle the republican troops were cut to pieces, after which Brutus killed himself. It was to the Church in this city that St. Paul wrote the epistle that still goes under their name. This place is still in being, though much decayed, and is the see of an archbishop. <div eID="gen44756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44757" type="x-p"/> The chief city of that part of Macedonia - This passage has greatly puzzled both critics and commentators. It is well known that, when Paulus Aemilius had conquered Macedonia, he divided it into four parts, μερη, and that he called the country that lay between the rivers Strymon and Nessus, the first part, and made Amphipolis its chief city, or metropolis; Philippi, therefore, was not its chief city. But Bishop Pearce has, with great show of reason, argued that, though Amphipolis was made the chief city of it by Paulus Aemilius, yet Philippi might have been the chief city in the days of St. Paul, which was two hundred and twenty years after the division by P. Aemilius. Besides, as it was at this place that Augustus gained that victory which put him in possession of the whole Roman empire, might not he have given to it that dignity which was before enjoyed by Amphipolis? This is the most rational way of solving this difficulty; and therefore I shall not trouble the reader with the different modes that have been proposed to alter and amend the Greek text. <div eID="gen44757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44758" type="x-p"/> And a colony - That is, a colony of Rome; for it appears that a colony was planted here by Julius Caesar, and afterwards enlarged by Augustus; the people, therefore, were considered as freemen of Rome, and, from this, call themselves Romans, <reference osisRef="Act.16.21">Act 16:21</reference>. The Jewish definition of קלניא kolonia (for they have the Latin word in Hebrew letters, as St. Luke has it. here, κολωνια, in Greek letters) is, a free city, which does not pay tribute.
entries.755081c1b724824921dd11e9da33bf87fef1949c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen44758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44759" type="x-p"/> By a river side, where prayer was wont to be made - Οὑ ενομιζετο προσευχη ειναι, where it was said there was a proseucha. The proseucha was a place of prayer, or a place used for worship, where there was no synagogue. It was a large building uncovered, with seats, as in an amphitheatre. Buildings of this sort the Jews had by the sea side, and by the sides of rivers. See this subject considered at large in the note on <reference osisRef="Luk.6.12">Luk 6:12</reference> (note). It appears that the apostles had heard from some of the Gentiles, or from some of the Jews themselves, that there was a place of prayer by the river side; and they went out in quest of it, knowing that, as it was the Sabbath, they should find some Jews there. <div eID="gen44759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44760" type="x-p"/> Spake unto the women - Probably this was before the time of their public worship, and while they were waiting for the assembling of the people in general; and Paul improved the opportunity to speak concerning Christ and salvation to the women that resorted thither.
entries.98aec0380c4eb4ba7f7a964fe38913b9e4e2f216: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen44760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44761" type="x-p"/> Lydia, a seller of purple - She probably had her name from the province of Lydia, in which the city of Thyatira was situated. The Lydian women have been celebrated for their beautiful purple manufactures. <div eID="gen44761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44762" type="x-p"/> Which worshipped God - That is, she was a proselyte to the Jewish religion; as were probably all the women that resorted hither. <div eID="gen44762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44763" type="x-p"/> Whose heart the Lord opened - As she was a sincere worshipper of God, she was prepared to receive the heavenly truths spoken by Paul and his companions; and, as she was faithful to the grace she had received, so God gave her more grace, and gave her now a Divine conviction that what was spoken by Paul was true; and therefore she attended unto the things - she believed them and received them as the doctrines of God; and in this faith she was joined by her whole family, and in it they were all baptized.
entries.36790cf9bc03f2fc833cc3ed39660355d2d0d8f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen44763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44764" type="x-p"/> If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord - The meaning seems to be this: If my present reception of the Gospel of Christ be a proof to you that I have been faithful to the Lord, in the light previously imparted, and that I am as likely to be faithful to this new grace as I have been to that already received, and, consequently, not likely by light or fickle conduct to bring any discredit on this Divine work, come into my house, and abide there. It is wrong to suppose that this woman had not received a measure of the light of God before this time. <div eID="gen44764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44765" type="x-p"/> And she constrained us - She used such entreaties and persuasions that at last they consented to lodge there.
entries.e87493c7b4e858303916ab074bae962468a7754e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen44765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44766" type="x-p"/> As we went to prayer - Εις προσευχην, Into the proseucha: see on <reference osisRef="Act.16.13">Act 16:13</reference> (note), and on <reference osisRef="Luk.6.12">Luk 6:12</reference> (note). The article, την, is added here by ABCE, several others, Origen and Theophylact: thus makes the place more emphatic, and seems to determine the above meaning of προσευχην to be right - not the act of prayer or praying to God, but the place, the oratory, in which these proselytes assembled for the purpose of praying, reading the law and the prophets, and such like exercises of devotion. It appears that the apostles spent dome time here; as it is evident, from this and the following verses, that they often resorted to this place to preach the Gospel. <div eID="gen44766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44767" type="x-p"/> Possessed with a spirit of divination - Εχουσαν πνευμα πυθωνος, Having a spirit of Python, or of Apollo. Pytho was, according to fable, a huge serpent, that had an oracle at Mount Parnassus, famous for predicting future events; Apollo slew this serpent, and hence he was called Pythius, and became celebrated as the foreteller of future events; and all those, who either could or pretended to predict future events, were influenced by the spirit of Apollo Pythius. As often-times the priestesses of this god became greatly agitated, and gave answers apparently from their bellies, when their mouths remained close, πυθων was applied to the εγγαϚριμυθοι, or ventriloquists. Hesychius defines πυθων, δαιμονιον μαντικον, a divining demon; and it was evidently such a one that possessed this young woman, and which Paul expelled, <reference osisRef="Act.16.18">Act 16:18</reference>. See on this subject the notes on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Deu.18.11">Deu 18:11</reference> (note). <div eID="gen44767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44768" type="x-p"/> Brought her masters much gain by soothsaying - Μαντευουενη, By divination, or what we call telling fortunes. Our term soothsaying coming from the Anglo-Saxon, truth, and to say, i.e. truth saying, or saying the truth. For, as it was supposed among the heathen that such persons spoke by the inspiration of their god, consequently what they said must be true. However, our translators might have used a term here that would not have been so creditable to this Pythoness; for, what she said concerning the apostles excepted, she certainly could not be supposed to tell the truth, while her inspiration came from him who is the father of lies. But Satan will sometimes conceal himself under the guise of truth, that he may the more effectually deceive. See below.
entries.57833432e09c9c158e0e3889687b16f8b4660b83: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen44768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44769" type="x-p"/> These men are the servants, etc. - It is astonishing how such a testimony could be given in such a case; every syllable of it true, and at the same time full, clear, and distinct. But mark the deep design and artifice of this evil spirit: <div eID="gen44769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44770" type="x-p"/> 1. He well knew that the Jewish law abhorred all magic, incantations, magical rites, and dealings with familiar spirits; he therefore bears what was in itself a true testimony to the apostles, that by it he may destroy their credit, and ruin their usefulness. The Jews, by this testimony, would be led at once to believe that the apostles were in compact with these demons, and that the miracles they wrought were done by the agency of these wicked spirits, and that the whole was the effect of magic; and this, of course, would harden their hearts against the preaching of the Gospel. <div eID="gen44770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44771" type="x-p"/> 2. The Gentiles, finding that their own demon bore testimony to the apostles, would naturally consider that the whole was one system; that they had nothing to learn, nothing to correct; and thus the preaching of the apostles must be useless to them. In such a predicament is this, nothing could have saved the credit of the apostles but their dispossessing this woman of her familiar spirit, and that in the most incontestable manner; for what could have saved the credit of Moses and Aaron, when the magicians of Egypt turned their rods into serpents, had not Aaron's rod devoured theirs? And what could have saved the credit of these apostles but the casting out of this spirit of divination, with which, otherwise, both Jews and Gentiles would have believed them in compact?
entries.78c8c1c1a1e47c42966457ab5cbe4a975bd97095: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen44771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44772" type="x-p"/> Paul, being grieved - Probably for the reasons assigned above. <div eID="gen44772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44773" type="x-p"/> Turned - to the spirit - Not to the woman; she was only the organ by which the spirit acted. <div eID="gen44773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44774" type="x-p"/> I command thee, in the name of Jesus - Jesus is the Savior; Satan is Abaddon and Apollyon, the destroyer. The sovereign Savior says to the destroyer, Come out of her; and he came out in the same hour. Every circumstance of this case proves it to have been a real possession. We have already had several opportunities of remarking the great accuracy of St. Luke in his accounts of demoniacs: his education as a physician gave him advantages to detect imposture of this kind where it subsisted; but he sees none in this case. He speaks of the spirit and the damsel as distinct persons. The damsel had a spirit of divination. Paul turned to the spirit, and said, I command Thee to come out of Her; and he came out in the same hour. Had not St. Luke considered this as a real case of diabolic possession, he has made use of the most improper language he could choose; language and forms of speech calculated to deceive all his readers, and cause them to believe a lie. But it is impossible that the holy apostle could do so, because he was a good man; and it is not likely he could be deceived by a parcel of charlatans, because he was a wise man; and it would be absurd to suppose that, while he was under the influence of the Holy Spirit, he could be imposed on by the cunning of even the devil himself.
